title: Listening Skills Training in Serbia
text:
Waitlist-controlled field experiment for social workers
    Listening Skills Training in Serbia

    • 20 Serbian municipalities (10 experimental, 10 control)
    • Four measurement occasions (T0–T3, January–December)
    • 451 social workers
    • 102 items & 23 preregistered scales
    • Three hypothesis blocks (H1 Listening & Togetherness → H2 Cognitive Complexity → H3 Well-being)

  

  
    Start
    
      
        Read me
        What this report documents and what each chapter holds.
        →
      
    
  

  
    Part A — Data
    
      
        From Questionnaires to the Analysis File
        79 Excel files, code corrections, double entries, and the case log.
        →
      
      
        Scales and Analysis Datasets
        Reverse coding, scale composites, long and wide data.
        →
      
      
        Sample
        Participants, waves, municipalities, and sample sets.
        →
      
      
        Data Quality
        Careless responding, two flags, and the search for double entries.
        →
      
    
  

  
    Part B — Measurement
    
      
        Reliability and Baseline Correlations
        Reliability per wave and correlations at baseline.
        →
      
      
        Measurement Models per Wave
        Confirmatory factor models at each wave (T0–T3).
        →
      
      
        Measurement Invariance over Time
        Configural, metric, and scalar invariance across the waves.
        →
      
      
        Simultaneous Block Models
        Block CFAs: discriminant validity and block-level invariance.
        →
      
    
  

  
    Part C — Training Effects (Preregistered)
    
      
        Means and Δd
        Means by condition and wave, and standardized change.
        →
      
      
        Multilevel Models
        Treatment effects, replication, and sensitivity.
        →
      
      
        Latent Difference-in-Differences
        Latent DiD in structured means models.
        →
      
      
        Serial Mediation
        Serial mediation chain: H1 → H2 → H3.
        →
      
      
        Movers
        Classification of individual change.
        →
      
      
        Robustness across Sample Sets
        The training effects on the sample sets S0 to S9.
        →
      
    
  

  
    Part D — Post Hoc
    
      
        Item Pruning
        Reduction and cleanup of the item pool.
        →
      
      
        Exploratory Graph Analysis
        Dimensional structure via network psychometrics.
        →
      
      
        Redundancy & IRT
        Redundancy analysis (UVA) and graded response models.
        →
      
      
        Final Structure
        The final item pool, its communities, factors and composites.
        →
      
      
        Training Effects on the New Structure
        Δd, multilevel models and mediation on the two factors.
        →
      
      
        Synthesis
        Integration of all findings.
        →
      
    
  

  
    Part E — Appendix
    
      
        Item-Level Δd
        The training effects item by item, ranked.
        →
      
      
        Software Versions
        R, Quarto and every package with its version.
        →
      
      
        Requests and Their Status
        What the team asked for, in plain words, and where it stands.
        →

What this report documents, how to read it, and what happens in each chapter. Computes nothing.

title: 0. Read me
text:
What each chapter contains
Part A: Data

From questionnaires to the analysis file. Reads the 79 Excel files returned by the municipalities, builds the participant codes, corrects codes that were mistyped, removes paper forms that were entered twice, and saves one analysis file.
Scales and analysis datasets. Reverse-codes negatively worded items, builds the 23 scale scores and the three hypothesis composites, and arranges the data one row per questionnaire and one row per person.
Sample. Who took part, at which waves and in which municipalities; whether the two conditions are comparable; the sample sets used to test robustness.
Data quality. Screens every questionnaire for careless responding and searches once more for forms entered twice.

Part B: Measurement

Reliability and baseline correlations. Internal consistency of every scale and composite at each wave, and how the scales relate before the training.
Measurement models per wave. Confirmatory factor analysis of every scale at each of the four waves.
Measurement invariance over time. Whether each scale measures the same construct in the same way at all four waves, the precondition for comparing means over time; judged by two sets of cutoffs, with partial invariance, approximate invariance (alignment) and a test across the two groups before the training.
Simultaneous block models. All scales of one hypothesis modelled together, to test whether they are distinct.

Part C: Training effects, as preregistered

Means and Δd. Means by condition and wave, and the standardized difference in change between the trained and the waiting group, with a second standard deviation, a correction for multiple testing and a look at dropout.
Multilevel models. The preregistered models of the training effect, with participants nested in municipalities and, as a check, in trainers; one-sided tests and a correction for multiple testing; the replication in the second round; random slopes; equivalence tests.
Latent difference-in-differences. The training effect on latent means, corrected for measurement error; with the control group’s change while it waits, a correction for multiple testing, a restricted model and the effects across the sample sets.
Serial mediation. Whether the training improves well-being through listening and cognitive complexity, with manifest composites and with latent blocks.
Movers. How many participants changed reliably, by condition.
Robustness. Every effect re-estimated in alternative samples: complete cases, attrition patterns, careless responding.

Part D: Post hoc

Item pruning. Which items were set aside, for ceiling effects or low responsiveness, and why.
Exploratory graph analysis. The dimensional structure of the item pool, estimated from the data.
Redundancy and IRT. Redundant items and item response models, also at each wave.
Final structure. The resulting item structure and its replication across the four waves.
Training effects on the new structure. The training effects re-estimated on the factors found in the data and on the single item on life satisfaction, and whether the factors are measured invariantly over time.
Synthesis. How the preregistered and the post hoc results fit together.

Part E: Appendix

Study 1. The train-the-trainer study with the 16 trainers; it follows once its data are available.
Item-level Δd. The training effect on every single item.
Software versions.
Requests and their status. What the team asked for in its e-mails, in plain words, and where each request stands.

title: 0. Read me
text:
The study
What was studied? Social workers in 20 Serbian municipalities took part in a listening training. Ten municipalities were trained between January and March 2025; the other ten waited and were trained between September and December 2025. Participants answered the same questionnaire up to four times: in January (T0), March (T1), September (T2) and December (T3). The analyses test whether the training improved listening and togetherness (H1), cognitive complexity (H2) and well-being (H3).

title: 0. Read me
text:
How to read this report
How do code and results relate?

Every chapter shows the code that produces its results, directly above them. Code that several chapters share is kept in a separate file and shown in full where it is used.
The text explains each step in plain language. Knowing R helps, but the logic can be followed without it.
Each chapter names the tables and sections of the paper its results feed.
Numbers that the paper reports are checked in the code: a hidden line stops the report if one of them changes.

Can the analyses be re-run? The questionnaires carry self-generated participant codes, ages and sex, so the data are not published with this report. The code is complete: every step can be followed and applied to comparable data.
Who is SW0123? Every person appears under a pseudonym: the respondent ID of the data deposit (SW0001 to SW0461, and SW0462 for the second of two people who shared one code), or T01 to T64 for a code that was typed at one wave and corrected later. The codes themselves, built from the mother’s name and birthday, never appear in this report.

title: 1. From Questionnaires to the Analysis File
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



How the 79 Excel files of the municipalities become one analysis file: reading the questionnaires, recognizing each person across the waves, correcting mistyped codes, removing paper forms entered more than once, and setting impossible answers to missing. Every correction is listed with its evidence. Feeds the description of the sample and of data processing in the Method section, and the table of deviations from the preregistration.

title: 1. From Questionnaires to the Analysis File
text:
1.1 Reading the questionnaires
What did the municipalities send? One Excel file per municipality and wave. Twenty municipalities and four waves would make 80 files; three waves never arrived (Lebane in March, Sokobanja and Valjevo in December), and Leskovac and Užice sent their December questionnaires in two files each: 79 files.

# The questionnaires: one Excel file per municipality and wave
# -> one row per questionnaire

# one fixed order on every computer: where a code leaves age or sex blank at
# one wave, it is filled from the questionnaire read first
excel_files <- list.files(raw_dir, pattern = "\\.xlsx$", full.names = TRUE) |>
  str_subset("/~\\$", negate = TRUE) |>   # not the lock files of open workbooks
  stri_sort(locale = "en_US")

if (length(excel_files) != 79) {
  stop("Expected the 79 Excel files in '", raw_dir, "', found ",
       length(excel_files), " (see data/README.md).", call. = FALSE)
}

# One file: the answers below three label rows (Serbian wording, an empty
# row, English wording), municipality and wave from the file name, e.g.
# "Arilje - Trainee Questionnaires - December 2025", empty rows dropped.
read_questionnaires <- \(file) {
  name  <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(file))
  month <- months_list[str_detect(name, regex(months_list, ignore_case = TRUE))]
  answers <- read_excel(file, .name_repair = "unique_quiet") |>
    mutate(across(where(is.character), enc2utf8)) |>
    slice(-(1:3)) |>
    mutate(Municipality = sub("Trainees.*", "", sub("^(.*?)-.*", "\\1", name)),
           Occasion     = month[1])
  answers[rowSums(is.na(answers)) < ncol(answers) - 2, ]
}

raw <- excel_files |>
  map(read_questionnaires) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  mutate(sex          = toupper(trimws(sex)),
         age          = as.numeric(age),
         Municipality = trimws(Municipality),
         Occasion     = trimws(Occasion))

# five files carry notes of the data entry in an unnamed extra column
entry_notes <- raw |>
  filter(!is.na(`...111`)) |>
  select(Municipality, Occasion, note = `...111`)

raw <- raw |> select(-`...111`)

1.4 Corrections made for this report
What did the checks of 2026 add? Four lists. The paper forms were not available, so every entry rests on the data; the evidence follows the lists.

# Corrections made for this report (November 2026); the evidence for each is
# shown in Chapter 1

# one person, two codes -> joined under one ID (the ID of the person joined)
code_merges <- tribble(
  ~municipality, ~code_from, ~code_to, ~source,
  # the code written a second time, at the end, names a person with other waves
  "Arilje",      "SW0163",   "SW0283", "second code entry",
  "Požarevac",   "SW0374",   "SW0368", "second code entry",
  "Raška",       "SW0397",   "SW0351", "second code entry",
  "NoviPazar",   "SW0186",   "SW0327", "second code entry",
  "Valjevo",     "SW0323",   "SW0353", "second code entry",
  # the Serbian letter Lj typed as "LJ" at one wave, as "L" at the others
  "Arilje",      "SW0250",   "SW0440", "spelling",
  "Sokobanja",   "SW0326",   "SW0167", "spelling",
  "Sokobanja",   "SW0160",   "SW0190", "spelling",
  # a Cyrillic A (U+0410), which looks like the Latin A of the other waves
  "Pirot",       "SW0312",   "SW0053", "spelling",
  # the day of birth left blank at one wave; same month, age and sex
  "Vršac",       "SW0408",   "SW0090", "missing day"
)

# two people, one code: round 5 joined T08 onto SW0337 and so put two
# January questionnaires on one person -> the second gets an own ID
code_splits <- tribble(
  ~code,    ~Occasion, ~age, ~new_code,
  "SW0337", 0,         54,   "SW0462"
)

# one paper form, entered twice -> the later entry is removed
double_entries <- tribble(
  ~code,    ~Occasion, ~same_form_as_code, ~same_form_as_occasion,
  "SW0206", 1,         "SW0206",           0,
  "SW0082", 3,         "SW0082",           2,
  "SW0402", 3,         "SW0402",           2,
  "SW0002", 3,         "SW0002",           2,
  "SW0210", 3,         "SW0210",           2,
  "SW0284", 3,         "SW0284",           2,
  "SW0225", 3,         "SW0225",           2,
  "SW0359", 3,         "SW0359",           2,
  "SW0208", 3,         "SW0208",           2,
  "SW0165", 1,         "SW0165",           0,
  "SW0209", 1,         "SW0209",           0,
  "SW0083", 3,         "SW0040",           2     # under a mistyped code
)

# answers outside the scale from 0 to 10, both in one December
# questionnaire -> missing (after the answers become numbers, 1.6)
out_of_range <- tribble(
  ~code,    ~Occasion, ~item,             ~value,
  "SW0385", 3,         "ParadoxMindset7", 20,
  "SW0385", 3,         "ParadoxMindset8", 20
)


Evidence

items <- names(select(x, ListenOther1:needSatisfaction24))

# Share of answers (in %) in which two questionnaires agree, counted over the
# items answered in both. Copies of one paper form agree in almost all answers.
share_identical <- \(a, b) {
  round(100 * mean(unlist(a[1, items]) == unlist(b[1, items]), na.rm = TRUE))
}

# One line per person: waves, age and sex.
describe_persons <- \(ids) {
  x |>
    filter(code %in% ids) |>
    summarise(waves = paste0("T", sort(unique(Occasion)), collapse = ", "),
              age   = paste(unique(age), collapse = "/"),
              sex   = paste(unique(sex), collapse = "/"),
              .by = code)
}

# Two persons' codes compared without showing them, on their first
# questionnaires: the parts that differ (letter, month, day), and whether the
# code written a second time, at the end of the first person's
# questionnaire, is the second person's code ("blank" if left empty).
compare_codes <- \(from, to) {
  a <- x |> filter(code == from) |> slice(1)
  b <- x |> filter(code == to) |> slice(1)
  start_a <- as.character(c(a$`Letter...1`, a$`Month...2`, a$`Day...3`))
  start_b <- as.character(c(b$`Letter...1`, b$`Month...2`, b$`Day...3`))
  end_a   <- as.character(c(a$`Letter...108`, a$`Month...109`, a$`Day...110`))
  differs <- c("letter", "month", "day")[!map2_lgl(start_a, start_b, identical)]
  tibble(parts_differ     = paste(differs, collapse = " and "),
         end_names_joined = case_when(all(is.na(end_a))        ~ "blank",
                                      identical(end_a, start_b) ~ "yes",
                                      TRUE                      ~ "no"))
}

For comparison: how far do one person’s answers agree between two waves? Over everyone who answered in March and in September, the median share:

both_waves <- intersect(x$code[x$Occasion == 1], x$code[x$Occasion == 2])

both_waves |>
  map_dbl(\(id) share_identical(filter(x, code == id, Occasion == 1),
                                filter(x, code == id, Occasion == 2))) |>
  median()

  left_join(describe_persons(code_merges$code_from),
            by = c(code_from = "code")) |>
  left_join(describe_persons(code_merges$code_to),
            by = c(code_to = "code"), suffix = c("", "_joined")) |>

  select(code_from, waves, age, sex, code_to, waves_joined, age_joined,

Applying the corrections

# The corrections of this report, applied after checking that every listed
# questionnaire is there exactly as listed; `case_log` records each one

# Stops with the listed codes that are not found exactly once; `listed`
# holds the columns that identify the questionnaire.
expect_once <- \(listed, what) {
  found   <- listed |> left_join(count(x, pick(all_of(names(listed)))),
                                 by = names(listed))
  missing <- found$code[is.na(found$n) | found$n != 1]
  if (length(missing) > 0) {
    stop(what, ": not found exactly once: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "),
         call. = FALSE)
  }
}

# Stops naming the codes, if any.
stop_if_any <- \(codes, what) {
  if (length(codes) > 0) {
    stop(what, ": ", paste(unique(codes), collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE)
  }
}

# the join list: every code exists, none is listed twice, none is both
# joined and a join target (no chains)
stop_if_any(setdiff(c(code_merges$code_from, code_merges$code_to), x$code),
            "Join: no questionnaire with the code")
stop_if_any(code_merges$code_from[duplicated(code_merges$code_from)],
            "Join: listed twice")
stop_if_any(intersect(code_merges$code_from, code_merges$code_to),
            "Join: joined and also a join target")

# a join must not give a person two questionnaires at one wave
clashes <- code_merges |>
  inner_join(distinct(x, code, Occasion), by = c(code_from = "code")) |>
  inner_join(distinct(x, code, Occasion), by = c(code_to = "code", "Occasion"))
stop_if_any(clashes$code_from,
            "Join: a questionnaire at the same wave as its join target")

expect_once(select(code_splits, code, Occasion, age), "Split")
expect_once(select(double_entries, code, Occasion), "Double entry")

# waves as T0 to T3; the waves of each code that a join replaces (for the log)
wave <- \(occasion) paste0("T", occasion)
joined_waves <- x |>
  filter(code %in% code_merges$code_from) |>
  summarise(wave = paste(wave(sort(unique(Occasion))), collapse = ", "),
            .by = code)

# codes that already have more than one questionnaire at a wave (copies of
# one form, see 1.5): joins and splits must not add to them, e.g. by joining
# two codes onto one
repeated_before <- x |> count(code, Occasion) |> filter(n > 1)

x <- x |>
  # one person, two codes -> one code
  left_join(select(code_merges, code = code_from, code_to), by = "code") |>
  mutate(code = coalesce(code_to, code)) |>
  select(-code_to) |>
  # two people, one code -> the second gets its own code back
  left_join(code_splits, by = c("code", "Occasion", "age")) |>
  mutate(code = coalesce(new_code, code)) |>
  select(-new_code)

repeated_after <- x |> count(code, Occasion) |> filter(n > 1)
new_repeats    <- repeated_after |>
  anti_join(repeated_before, by = c("code", "Occasion"))
stop_if_any(new_repeats$code, "Join: two questionnaires at one wave for")

# one form, entered twice -> the later entry removed
n_before <- nrow(x)
x <- x |> anti_join(double_entries, by = c("code", "Occasion"))
if (n_before - nrow(x) != nrow(double_entries)) {
  stop("Double entry: removed ", n_before - nrow(x), " entries, listed ",
       nrow(double_entries), call. = FALSE)
}

case_log <- bind_rows(
  code_merges |>
    left_join(joined_waves, by = c(code_from = "code")) |>
    transmute(correction = "codes joined", code = code_from, wave,
              change = paste("now", code_to)),
  code_splits |>
    transmute(correction = "code split", code, wave = wave(Occasion),
              change = paste("one questionnaire now", new_code)),
  double_entries |>
    transmute(correction = "double entry removed", code, wave = wave(Occasion),
              change = paste("same form as", same_form_as_code,
                             wave(same_form_as_occasion)))
)

section: 1.5 One questionnaire per person and wave

1.5 One questionnaire per person and wave
Why does a code still appear twice at one wave? The two December files of Leskovac and of Užice overlap, and a few forms were typed more than once. Each code and wave with more than one entry, and how far the further entries agree with the first:

# the lowest agreement of the further entries with the first
copies_agree <- \(entries) {
  map_dbl(2:nrow(entries), \(i) share_identical(entries[1, ], entries[i, ])) |>
    min()
}

repeated <- x |>
  filter(rowSums(is.na(pick(all_of(items)))) < 70) |>   # not the empty SW0429
  filter(n() > 1, .by = c(code, Occasion)) |>
  summarise(entries   = n(),
            identical = copies_agree(pick(all_of(items))),
            .by = c(code, Occasion, Municipality))

All are copies of one form: one entry each is kept. A questionnaire of SW0429 is empty apart from its code and is dropped.

# One questionnaire per person and wave

x <- x |>
  # one questionnaire of SW0429 is empty apart from its code
  filter(!(code == "SW0429" & rowSums(is.na(across(everything()))) >= 70)) |>
  # copies of one form (overlapping December files of Leskovac and Užice, forms
  # typed twice) -> the entry with the fewest missing answers
  group_by(code, Occasion) |>
  slice_min(order_by = rowSums(is.na(across(everything()))),
            n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

# Item answers

x <- x |>
  mutate(
    # three answers typed with extra digits -> the value meant
    Resonance1            = as.numeric(Resonance1) |>
                            rec(rules = "1010=10; else=copy"),
    IntellectualHumility6 = as.numeric(IntellectualHumility6) |>
                            rec(rules = "100=10; else=copy"),
    needSatisfaction21    = as.numeric(needSatisfaction21) |>
                            rec(rules = "99=9; else=copy")
  ) |>
  # the files cut the last letter of this item name
  rename_with(\(name) sub("IntellectualCapita", "IntellectualCapital", name)) |>
  # the 102 items; entries that are not one number ("7 or 8", "no answ.")
  # -> missing
  mutate(across(ListenOther1:needSatisfaction24,
                \(answer) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(answer))))

Which answers lie outside the scale? Two answers of 20 on the scale from 0 to 10, both in one December questionnaire, listed in 1.4:

# Answers outside the scale from 0 to 10 -> missing; the listed answers must
# be exactly the answers above 10 in the file

above_10 <- x |>
  select(code, Occasion, ListenOther1:needSatisfaction24) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(code, Occasion), names_to = "item") |>
  filter(value > 10)

listed <- c("code", "Occasion", "item", "value")
stop_if_any(c(anti_join(above_10, out_of_range, by = listed)$code,
              anti_join(out_of_range, above_10, by = listed)$code),
            "Out of range: listed and found answers above 10 differ for")

x <- x |> set_na(ParadoxMindset7 = 20, ParadoxMindset8 = 20, tag = FALSE)

case_log <- case_log |>
  bind_rows(out_of_range |>
              transmute(correction = "answer set to missing", code,
                        wave   = wave(Occasion),
                        change = paste(item, "was", value)))

title: 1. From Questionnaires to the Analysis File
text:
1.7 Waves attended
Which waves did each person attend? Six marks per person, used in Chapter 3 to define the sample sets.

# Waves attended: six marks per person, stored with each of the person's
# questionnaires (sample sets, Chapter 3)

patterns <- x |>
  arrange(code, Occasion) |>
  summarise(pattern      = paste(sort(unique(Occasion)), collapse = "-"),
            Municipality = first(Municipality),
            .by = code) |>
  mutate(Group = if_else(Municipality %in% trained_first,
                         "Trained First", "Trained Second"))

sample_flags <- patterns |>
  mutate(
    # all four waves; at least two; January; not January only
    s1_complete       = pattern == "0-1-2-3",
    s2_no_singletons  = nchar(gsub("[^-]", "", pattern)) >= 1,
    s3_has_T0         = grepl("^0", pattern),
    # January and a wave after the own training
    s4_T0_plus_post   = case_when(
      Group == "Trained First"  ~ grepl("^0", pattern) &
                                  grepl("[1-3]", gsub("^0", "", pattern)),
      Group == "Trained Second" ~ grepl("^0", pattern) & grepl("3", pattern)
    ),
    # the waves right before and after the own training
    s5_group_baseline = case_when(
      Group == "Trained First"  ~ grepl("^0", pattern) & grepl("1", pattern),
      Group == "Trained Second" ~ grepl("2", pattern) & grepl("3", pattern)
    ),
    s6_no_T0_dropouts = pattern != "0"
  )

x <- x |>
  select(-matches("^s[1-6]_")) |>
  left_join(select(sample_flags, code, matches("^s[1-6]_")), by = "code")

title: 1. From Questionnaires to the Analysis File
text:
1.2 Participant codes
How is a person recognized across the waves? Participants gave no names. They formed a code from the third letter of their mother’s first name and the month and day of her birth, completed by the first two letters of the municipality. The same code at two waves marks the same person, so a code typed differently at one wave makes one person look like two.

# Municipalities, waves, participant codes, condition

x <- raw |>
  mutate(
    # municipality names as in the file names -> one spelling, with diacritics
    Municipality = gsub(" ", "", Municipality),
    Municipality = case_when(
      Municipality == "Arlje"                   ~ "Arilje",
      Municipality == "Bac"                     ~ "Bač",
      Municipality %in% c("Kanijza", "Kanjiza") ~ "Kanjiža",
      Municipality == "Uzice"                   ~ "Užice",
      Municipality == "Sabac"                   ~ "Šabac",
      Municipality == "Vrsac"                   ~ "Vršac",
      Municipality == "Pozarevac"               ~ "Požarevac",
      Municipality %in% c("SID", "Sid")         ~ "Šid",
      Municipality == "Krusevac"                ~ "Kruševac",
      Municipality == "Raska"                   ~ "Raška",
      TRUE                                      ~ Municipality
    ),
    Municipality = stri_trans_nfc(Municipality),   # one form for č, š, ž
    # wave: 0 = January (T0), 1 = March, 2 = September, 3 = December (T3)
    Occasion    = match(Occasion, months_list) - 1,
    `Month...2` = as.numeric(`Month...2`),
    `Day...3`   = as.numeric(`Day...3`),
    age         = as.numeric(age)
  )

# The participant code: third letter of the mother's first name, month and day
# of her birth, first two letters of the municipality, e.g. "M315Ar". The
# questionnaire asks for it twice, at the start (columns 1-3) and at the end
# (columns 108-110); the code is built from the first.
x <- x |>
  mutate(
    # Serbian letters with diacritics -> plain letters
    `Letter...1` = gsub("Ž", "Z", `Letter...1`),
    `Letter...1` = gsub("Š", "S", `Letter...1`),
    `Letter...1` = gsub("Đ", "D", `Letter...1`),
    muni_prefix  = stri_trans_general(Municipality, "Latin-ASCII") |>
                   substr(1, 2),
    code         = paste0(`Letter...1`, `Month...2`, `Day...3`, muni_prefix)
  )

x <- x |>
  # age or sex left blank at one wave -> from the same code's other waves
  group_by(code) |>
  fill(age, sex, .direction = "downup") |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(condition = if_else(Municipality %in% trained_first,
                             "Experimental", "Control"))

How often do the two codes of a questionnaire agree? The code is asked for at the start and again at the end of the questionnaire. Before anything is corrected, the two are compared wherever both were filled in:

# the second code, written like the first (letters without diacritics)
code_twice <- x |>
  transmute(first  = str_c(toupper(`Letter...1`), `Month...2`, `Day...3`),
            second = str_c(toupper(chartr("ŽŠĐ", "ZSD", `Letter...108`)),
                           as.numeric(`Month...109`),
                           as.numeric(`Day...110`))) |>
  filter(!is.na(first), !is.na(second))
code_twice |> summarise(both_given = n(), disagree = sum(first != second))





both_given
disagree




1109
27






The two codes disagree on 27 of 1109 questionnaires. The code is built from the first entry only, and the second never overwrites it. Whether a code differs because the participant wrote it differently or because it was typed differently cannot be told apart without the paper forms; the partner organisation checked the data entry twice. A pseudonym therefore stands for a code, not for a verified person: someone who wrote their code very differently at two waves still counts as two people.
Why pseudonyms? A code consists of the mother’s initial and birthday; together with age and sex it could identify a social worker in a small office. From here on every person is known by a pseudonym only: the respondent ID of the data deposit (SW0001 to SW0461), or T01 to T64 for a code that was typed at one wave and corrected later. The file that links codes and pseudonyms stays private, and no code appears in this report. The column code holds the pseudonym from here on; it becomes id in 1.8.

# Pseudonyms: from here on every person is known by a pseudonym. A code is
# built from the mother's name and birthday and, with age and sex, could
# identify a person; the private file data/pseudonyms.csv (not published)
# links each code to its pseudonym

pseudonyms <- read_csv(pseudonym_file, show_col_types = FALSE)

missing_pseudonyms <- setdiff(x$code, pseudonyms$code)
if (length(missing_pseudonyms) > 0) {
  stop(length(missing_pseudonyms), " codes have no pseudonym; ",
       "run scripts/make_pseudonyms.R", call. = FALSE)
}

x <- x |>
  left_join(pseudonyms, by = "code") |>
  mutate(code = pseudonym) |>
  select(-pseudonym)

1.3 Mistyped codes
Which codes were corrected before this report, and on what grounds? Codes that differ in one letter or digit, within a municipality and with the same age and sex, were set to one spelling. The corrections were found in five rounds between December 2025 and February 2026.

# Mistyped codes, corrected in five rounds (December 2025 to February 2026):
# codes that differ in one letter or digit, within a municipality and with the
# same age and sex, are set to one spelling; `mistyped` names the part of the
# code that differed (the letter, the month or the day)

# two codes that stood for more than one person -> told apart by sex and age
x <- x |>
  mutate(code = case_when(
    code == "SW0289" & sex == "M" & age == 43 ~ "SW0126",
    code == "SW0289" & sex == "F" & age == 24 ~ "SW0333",
    code == "T01"    & sex == "F" & age == 44 ~ "T62",
    code == "T01"    & sex == "F" & age == 56 ~ "SW0049",
    TRUE                                     ~ code
  ))

title: 2. Scales and Analysis Datasets
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



The two datasets of all later chapters: one row per questionnaire (df) and one row per person (df_wide). Reverse-keyed items, the 23 preregistered scales and their scores, the three hypothesis composites, and the design variables of the models. Feeds the description of the measures in the Method section and Table 1.
source("R/packages.R")                  # all packages (Chapter 1)
source("R/settings.R")                  # waves, conditions, folders (Chapter 1)
x <- readRDS("cache/data_clean.rds")    # the analysis file (Chapter 1)

title: 2. Scales and Analysis Datasets
text:
2.1 Items
Which items point the other way? Every item is answered from 0 to 10. For 22 items a high answer means less of the construct, such as “I feel isolated” for togetherness; they are turned around (10 − x), so that high always means more. The 24 need-satisfaction items alternate between six subscales and are named by them.

# Items: reverse-keyed items turned around, the need-satisfaction block named
# by its six subscales, and the design columns as factors

# the 22 reverse-keyed items: 10 - x on the scale from 0 to 10
reverse_items <- c(
  "Alienation1", "Alienation2", "Isolation1", "Isolation2",
  "Flourishing5", "Flourishing6",
  "Rogerian7", "Rogerian8", "Rogerian9",
  "ToleranceDiversity1",
  paste0("needSatisfaction", seq(2, 24, by = 2))
)

# old name = new name; the 24 need-satisfaction items rotate through the six
# subscales (item 1 autonomy satisfaction, 2 autonomy non-frustration, ...,
# 7 autonomy satisfaction again)
need <- \(numbers) paste0("needSatisfaction", numbers)
rename_map <- c(
  "Alienation1" = "NoAlienation1", "Alienation2" = "NoAlienation2",
  "Isolation1"  = "NoIsolation1",  "Isolation2"  = "NoIsolation2",
  set_names(paste0("AutonomySatisfaction",     1:4), need(c(1, 7, 13, 19))),
  set_names(paste0("AutonomyNonFrustrated",    1:4), need(c(2, 8, 14, 20))),
  set_names(paste0("RelatednessSatisfaction",  1:4), need(c(3, 9, 15, 21))),
  set_names(paste0("RelatednessNonFrustrated", 1:4), need(c(4, 10, 16, 22))),
  set_names(paste0("CompetenceSatisfaction",   1:4), need(c(5, 11, 17, 23))),
  set_names(paste0("CompetenceNonFrustrated",  1:4), need(c(6, 12, 18, 24)))
)

df <- x |>
  mutate(across(all_of(reverse_items), \(answer) 10 - answer)) |>
  rename_with(\(old) rename_map[old], all_of(names(rename_map))) |>
  mutate(
    Occasion  = factor(Occasion, levels = 0:3, labels = paste0("T", 0:3)),
    # Control first: group 1 in the multi-group models
    condition = factor(condition, levels = c("Control", "Experimental")),
    # "NO ANSW." and "." -> missing
    sex       = case_match(sex, "F" ~ "Female", "M" ~ "Male")
  )

# the 102 items, from the first listening to the last need-satisfaction item
item_names <- names(select(df, ListenOther1:CompetenceNonFrustrated4))


length(item_names)

[1] 102

title: 2. Scales and Analysis Datasets
text:
2.2 The 23 scales
Which items make up each scale? The preregistration groups 23 scales into three hypothesis blocks: listening and togetherness (H1), cognitive complexity (H2) and well-being (H3).

# The 23 preregistered scales, their labels and hypothesis blocks; needs
# `item_names` (the 102 items, Chapter 2)

scales <- tribble(
  ~scale,                     ~label,                       ~block,
  # H1: listening and togetherness
  "ListenOther",              "Others Listen to Me",        "H1",
  "ListenSelf",               "I Listen",                   "H1",
  "Understood",               "Understood",                 "H1",
  "KamaMuta",                 "Kama Muta",                  "H1",
  "Resonance",                "Positivity Resonance",       "H1",
  "Belongingness",            "Belongingness",              "H1",
  "NoAlienation",             "No Alienation",              "H1",
  "NoIsolation",              "No Isolation",               "H1",
  # H2: cognitive complexity
  "Rogerian",                 "Rogerian Schema",            "H2",
  "ParadoxMindset",           "Paradox Mindset",            "H2",
  "IntellectualHumility",     "Intellectual Humility",      "H2",
  "ToleranceDiversity",       "Tolerance Diversity",        "H2",
  "womenAttitude",            "Women Attitude",             "H2",
  # H3: well-being
  "Flourishing",              "Flourishing",                "H3",
  "AutonomySatisfaction",     "Autonomy Satisfaction",      "H3",
  "RelatednessSatisfaction",  "Relatedness Satisfaction",   "H3",
  "CompetenceSatisfaction",   "Competence Satisfaction",    "H3",
  "AutonomyNonFrustrated",    "Autonomy Non-Frustrated",    "H3",
  "RelatednessNonFrustrated", "Relatedness Non-Frustrated", "H3",
  "CompetenceNonFrustrated",  "Competence Non-Frustrated",  "H3",
  "Empowerment",              "Empowerment",                "H3",
  "Agency",                   "Agency",                     "H3",
  "IntellectualCapital",      "Intellectual Capital",       "H3"
)

h1_scales <- scales$scale[scales$block == "H1"]
h2_scales <- scales$scale[scales$block == "H2"]
h3_scales <- scales$scale[scales$block == "H3"]

# the items of each scale: the scale name and a number, e.g. ListenOther1
scale_items <- scales$scale |>
  set_names() |>
  map(\(s) str_subset(item_names, paste0("^", s, "[0-9]+$")))

# women's attitude items 6 and 7 sit at the ceiling (T0 means above 9.7, see
# 2.3): left out of the score and of the H2 composite
ceiling_items <- c("womenAttitude6", "womenAttitude7")

# the pooled items of each hypothesis block
h1_items <- list_c(scale_items[h1_scales])
h2_items <- list_c(scale_items[h2_scales]) |> setdiff(ceiling_items)
h3_items <- list_c(scale_items[h3_scales])


scales |>
  mutate(items = lengths(scale_items))

title: 2. Scales and Analysis Datasets
text:
2.3 Scale scores
How is a scale scored? As the mean of its items, if at least one is answered. The three hypothesis composites pool all items of their block into one mean, rather than averaging the scale scores, so that a scale with more items weighs more.

# Scale scores: the mean of a scale's items (at least one answered); the
# women's attitude score also with all nine items; and the three hypothesis
# composites, the mean of the pooled items of their block

scores <- scale_items |>
  map(\(items) row_means(df[setdiff(items, ceiling_items)], min_valid = 1))

composites <- list(H1_ListeningTogetherness = h1_items,
                   H2_CognitiveComplexity   = h2_items,
                   H3_Wellbeing             = h3_items) |>
  map(\(items) row_means(df[items], min_valid = 1))

df <- df |>
  bind_cols(scores) |>
  mutate(womenAttitude_full = row_means(pick(all_of(scale_items$womenAttitude)),
                                        min_valid = 1),
         .after = womenAttitude) |>
  bind_cols(composites)

title: 2. Scales and Analysis Datasets
text:
2.4 Design variables
How do the models know who was trained when? Each municipality had one of ten trainers; each trainer trained one municipality of each condition. The codings of time and training, one line per condition and wave:

# Design variables: the trainer of each municipality (each trainer trained
# one municipality of each condition) and the codings of time and training
# that the multilevel models use (Chapter 10)

trainers <- tribble(
  ~trainer, ~trained_first, ~trained_second,
  1,        "Kula",         "Vršac",
  2,        "Valjevo",      "Bač",
  3,        "Sokobanja",    "Prijepolje",
  4,        "Leskovac",     "Arilje",
  5,        "Kruševac",     "Pirot",
  6,        "Šid",          "Požarevac",
  7,        "Raška",        "Šabac",
  8,        "NoviPazar",    "Lebane",
  9,        "Užice",        "Kikinda",
  10,       "Kanjiža",      "Vlasotince"
)

trainer_of <- trainers |>
  pivot_longer(c(trained_first, trained_second), values_to = "Municipality") |>
  transmute(Municipality, trainedBy = factor(trainer))

df <- df |>
  left_join(trainer_of, by = "Municipality") |>
  mutate(
    # 1 once the person's own group is trained: experimental from T1,
    # control at T3
    D = as.integer((condition == "Experimental" & Occasion != "T0") |
                   (condition == "Control"      & Occasion == "T3")),
    # piecewise time: the first training (from T1), the second training (T3)
    Time_Exp_Training     = ifelse(Occasion == "T0", 0, 1),
    Time_Control_Training = ifelse(Occasion == "T3", 1, 0),
    # Helmert contrasts: T0 against the later waves, T3 against the earlier
    TF_helmert = ifelse(Occasion == "T0", -3, 1),
    TS_helmert = ifelse(Occasion == "T3",  3, -1)
  )


df |>
  distinct(condition, Occasion, D, Time_Exp_Training, Time_Control_Training,
           TF_helmert, TS_helmert) |>
  arrange(condition, Occasion)

NoteAbout this chapter



Who took part, at which waves and in which municipalities; whether the two conditions are comparable; and the sample sets on which later chapters re-estimate the training effects. Feeds the description of the participants in the Method section.
source("R/packages.R")                  # all packages (Chapter 1)

title: 3. Sample
text:
3.1 Participants
Who took part? One row per person: the number of persons, their mean age, the share of women (of those who gave their sex) and the number of waves attended, by condition.

  summarise(persons = n(),
            age_M   = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE),
            age_SD  = sd(age, na.rm = TRUE),
            female  = mean(female, na.rm = TRUE),
            waves_M = mean(n_waves),
            .by = condition) |>
  arrange(condition) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))

title: 3. Sample
text:
3.3 Municipalities and trainers
How are the municipalities paired? The study randomized municipalities, not persons: each of ten trainers trained one municipality of each condition. certified is the number of participants the trainers reported as having completed the training; surveyed counts the persons who answered at least one questionnaire.

# completed trainings, as reported by the trainers
certified <- tribble(

title: 3. Sample
text:
3.6 Sample sets
On which samples are the effects re-estimated? Because persons entered and left the study at different waves, the training effects are re-estimated on nested sample sets (Chapter 14). Chapter 1 marks each questionnaire with the sets its person belongs to. S7, the set without the paper forms entered twice, equals S0, because Chapter 1 already removes them from the analysis file. Chapter 4 adds two sets from the screening for careless responding (S8, S9).

sample_sets <- tribble(
  ~set, ~flag,               ~definition,
  "S0", NA,                  "all questionnaires",
  "S1", "s1_complete",       "persons with all four waves",
  "S2", "s2_no_singletons",  "persons with at least two waves",
  "S3", "s3_has_T0",         "persons with a January questionnaire",
  "S4", "s4_T0_plus_post",   "January and a wave after the own training",
  "S5", "s5_group_baseline", "both waves around the own training",
  "S6", "s6_no_T0_dropouts", "not January only",
  "S7", NA,                  "without the forms entered twice (= S0)"
)

title: 4. Data quality
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Screens every questionnaire for careless answering with four indicators, combines them into two flags and turns the flags into the sample sets S8 and S9, on which Chapter 14 re-estimates the training effects. No questionnaire is removed here. The chapter also repeats the search for questionnaires entered twice on the analysis file. Feeds the data-quality paragraph of the Method section and the robustness table.
source("R/packages.R")                  # all packages (Chapter 1)
source("R/settings.R")                  # waves, conditions, folders (Chapter 1)
df      <- readRDS("cache/df.rds")      # one row per questionnaire (Chapter 2)
df_wide <- readRDS("cache/df_wide.rds") # one row per person (Chapter 2)
item_names <- names(select(df, ListenOther1:CompetenceNonFrustrated4))
source("R/scales.R")                    # the 23 scales (Chapter 2)

title: 4. Data quality
text:
4.1 The answers as given
Which answers are screened? Most indicators of careless answering look at the answers as they were ticked, in the order of the questionnaire. Chapter 2 turned the 22 reverse-keyed items around; for the screening they are turned back. keyed holds the items as analysed, answers the answers as given. The columns of the data follow the order of the printed Serbian questionnaire.

# the 22 reverse-keyed items, under their names from Chapter 2
reversed_items <- c("NoAlienation1", "NoAlienation2",
                    "NoIsolation1", "NoIsolation2",
                    "Flourishing5", "Flourishing6", paste0("Rogerian", 7:9),
                    "ToleranceDiversity1",
                    str_subset(item_names, "NonFrustrated"))

# one row per questionnaire, the 102 items in the order of the questionnaire
keyed   <- df |> select(all_of(item_names))
answers <- keyed |> mutate(across(all_of(reversed_items), \(x) 10 - x))

title: 4. Data quality
text:
4.2 Long strings
Did someone tick the same number again and again? A long string is a run of identical answers in the order of the questionnaire; a missing answer ends a run. Runs of agreement are plausible within a block of similar items, so the flag only counts runs that pass a reverse-keyed item, where an attentive person would switch sides.

# runs of identical answers; a missing answer ends a run
runs <- \(answer) {
  r <- rle(replace_na(answer, -1))
  tibble(length = r$lengths, value = r$values, end = cumsum(r$lengths)) |>
    mutate(start = end - length + 1) |>
    filter(value != -1)
}

# the longest run; with `through`, only runs that pass one of these item
# positions (0 if none does)
longest_run <- \(answer, through = NULL) {
  r <- runs(answer)
  if (nrow(r) == 0) return(NA_integer_)
  if (!is.null(through)) {
    r <- filter(r, map2_lgl(start, end, \(s, e) any(between(through, s, e))))
  }
  max(c(0L, r$length))
}

reversed_at    <- which(item_names %in% reversed_items)
answer_rows    <- as.matrix(answers) |> asplit(1) |> map(as.vector)
ls_any         <- map_int(answer_rows, longest_run)
ls_reversed    <- map_int(answer_rows, longest_run, through = reversed_at)

Where to draw the line? Questionnaires with a run of at least k items:

tibble(run_of_at_least = c(10, 15, 20, 25, 30)) |>
  mutate(any_items        = map_int(run_of_at_least, \(k) sum(ls_any >= k,
                                                                na.rm = TRUE)),
         through_reversed = map_int(run_of_at_least, \(k) sum(ls_reversed >= k,

title: 4. Data quality
text:
4.3 Agreeing with opposites
Did someone agree with an item and with its opposite? Six blocks mix positively and negatively worded items. Whoever agrees with the positive items should disagree with the negative ones, so that the mean of the positive and the mean of the negative answers add up to about 10. The inconsistency of a block is the distance of that sum from 10.

mixed_blocks <- list(
  Rogerian    = list(positive = paste0("Rogerian", 1:6),
                     negative = paste0("Rogerian", 7:9)),
  Flourishing = list(positive = paste0("Flourishing", c(1:4, 7)),
                     negative = paste0("Flourishing", 5:6)),
  Tolerance   = list(positive = paste0("ToleranceDiversity", 2:5),
                     negative = "ToleranceDiversity1"),
  Autonomy    = list(positive = paste0("AutonomySatisfaction", 1:4),
                     negative = paste0("AutonomyNonFrustrated", 1:4)),
  Relatedness = list(positive = paste0("RelatednessSatisfaction", 1:4),
                     negative = paste0("RelatednessNonFrustrated", 1:4)),
  Competence  = list(positive = paste0("CompetenceSatisfaction", 1:4),
                     negative = paste0("CompetenceNonFrustrated", 1:4))
)

# |mean of the positive + mean of the negative answers - 10|, per block
block_mean <- \(items) rowMeans(answers[items], na.rm = TRUE)
inconsistency <- mixed_blocks |>
  map(\(b) abs(block_mean(b$positive) + block_mean(b$negative) - 10)) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) if_else(is.finite(x), x, NA)))

# distance from the block's own mean, in SD of the block
inconsistency_z <- inconsistency |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) as.vector(scale(x))))

How inconsistent is a block usually? A block counts as inconsistent when it lies 2.5 SD above its own mean:

tibble(block  = names(mixed_blocks),
       M      = map_dbl(inconsistency, \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
       SD     = map_dbl(inconsistency, \(x) sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
       cutoff = M + 2.5 * SD,
       above  = map_int(inconsistency_z, \(z) sum(z >= 2.5, na.rm = TRUE))) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))

title: 4. Data quality
text:
4.4 Even-odd consistency
Do the two halves of each scale tell the same story? Each of the 22 multi-item scales is split into its odd and its even items. Across the scales, an attentive person’s odd-half means follow their even-half means. The index is the correlation of the two within the person, stepped up to full length with the Spearman-Brown formula. It needs at least ten scales with both halves.

# the scale of an item is its name without the number; 22 of the 23 scales
# have at least two items (Understood has one)
scale_of <- str_remove(item_names, "[0-9]+$")
items_by_scale <- split(item_names, scale_of) |>
  keep(\(items) length(items) >= 2)

half_means <- \(half) items_by_scale |>
  map(\(items) rowMeans(keyed[items[half(seq_along(items))]], na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  as_tibble()
odd  <- half_means(\(i) i %% 2 == 1)
even <- half_means(\(i) i %% 2 == 0)

# the correlation of the two halves within one questionnaire
halves_r <- \(a, b) {
  ok <- is.finite(a) & is.finite(b)
  if (sum(ok) < 10 || sd(a[ok]) == 0 || sd(b[ok]) == 0) return(NA_real_)
  cor(a[ok], b[ok])
}
r_halves <- map_dbl(seq_len(nrow(keyed)),
                    \(i) halves_r(unlist(odd[i, ]), unlist(even[i, ])))
even_odd <- if_else(r_halves <= -1, -1, 2 * r_halves / (1 + r_halves))

tibble(even_odd) |> describe(even_odd)

title: 4. Data quality
text:
4.5 Psychometric synonyms
Are items that go together answered together? Item pairs that correlate at .60 or more across all questionnaires are psychometric synonyms. Within a questionnaire, the answers to the first and to the second item of these pairs should correlate as well.

synonyms <- psychsyn(keyed, critval = .60, diag = TRUE, resample_na = FALSE)
synonyms |> describe(cor, numPairs)


Descriptive Statistics
----------------------

      cor  0.755  0.797 0.183  1.074 0.224   -1.350 1136       4
 numPairs 36.550 37.000 1.992 37.000 0.000   -9.587 1140       0

18 questionnaires fall below .22. The mirror index, psychometric antonyms, cannot be computed: no pair of items correlates at −.60 or below.

title: 4. Data quality
text:
4.6 Supplementary indicators
What else stands out? Three indicators are reported but do not enter the flags. An unusual profile (Mahalanobis distance) may be careless or just unusual; low variability across all answers (intra-individual response variability, IRV) may be honest agreement with everything; and many missing items are shown as missing anyway.

# Mahalanobis distance: missing answers replaced by the item median, for
# questionnaires with at most ten missing items
n_missing <- rowSums(is.na(keyed))
imputed   <- keyed |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) replace_na(x, median(x, na.rm = TRUE))))
mahad_p   <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(keyed))
mahad_p[n_missing <= 10] <- imputed[n_missing <= 10, ] |>
  mahad(plot = FALSE) |>
  pchisq(df = ncol(keyed), lower.tail = FALSE)

irv_all <- apply(answers, 1, sd, na.rm = TRUE)

tibble(indicator = c("Mahalanobis p < .001",
                     "IRV below the 2.5th percentile",
                     "more than 25 missing items"),
       questionnaires = c(sum(mahad_p < .001, na.rm = TRUE),
                          sum(irv_all < quantile(irv_all, .025, na.rm = TRUE),
                              na.rm = TRUE),

4.7 Two flags
Which questionnaires are flagged? The four indicators describe three behaviours: long strings, agreeing with opposites, and inconsistent profiles (even-odd or synonyms). The lenient flag marks questionnaires with any of the four indicators, the strict flag those with at least two of the three behaviours.

  select(id, Occasion, condition, Municipality) |>
  mutate(ls_reversed, blocks_inconsistent, even_odd,
         synonyms  = synonyms$cor,
         flag_ls   = ls_reversed >= 20 & !is.na(ls_reversed),
         flag_rev  = blocks_inconsistent >= 2,
         flag_eo   = even_odd < .30 & !is.na(even_odd),
         flag_syn  = synonyms < .22 & !is.na(synonyms),
         careless_any    = flag_ls | flag_rev | flag_eo | flag_syn,
         careless_strict = flag_ls + flag_rev + (flag_eo | flag_syn) >= 2)

title: 4. Data quality
text:
4.9 Questionnaires entered twice
Are there still questionnaires entered twice? Chapter 1 removed twelve paper forms that had been typed in twice. The same search, run again on the analysis file, compares every pair of questionnaires: pairs that agree on at least 95 % of the items both answered (and at least 80 items) are near duplicates. Varied answers make a chance match unlikely; a pair of extreme or uniform answer patterns can match by chance.

items <- as.matrix(answers)
near  <- map(seq_len(nrow(items) - 1), \(i) {
  later    <- items[(i + 1):nrow(items), , drop = FALSE]
  same     <- sweep(later, 2, items[i, ], "==")
  compared <- rowSums(!is.na(same))
  agree    <- rowSums(same, na.rm = TRUE)
  hit      <- which(compared >= 80 & agree / compared >= .95)
  tibble(i = i, j = i + hit, compared = compared[hit], agree = agree[hit])
}) |>
  list_rbind()

distinct_values <- apply(items, 1, \(a) n_distinct(a[!is.na(a)]))
extreme_percent <- 100 * rowMeans(items == 0 | items == 10, na.rm = TRUE)

near <- near |>
  mutate(id_A = df$id[i], wave_A = df$Occasion[i],
         id_B = df$id[j], wave_B = df$Occasion[j],
         distinct = pmin(distinct_values[i], distinct_values[j]),
         extreme  = round(pmax(extreme_percent[i], extreme_percent[j])),
         evidence = if_else(
           (extreme < 60 & distinct >= 8) |
             (agree == compared & compared >= 100 & distinct >= 5),
           "entered twice", "extreme pattern")) |>
  select(id_A, wave_A, id_B, wave_B, compared, agree, distinct, extreme,
         evidence)

title: 7. Measurement invariance over time
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Tests for each of the 22 latent constructs whether the questionnaire measures it the same way at all four waves: the same structure (configural), the same loadings (metric) and the same intercepts (scalar), judged by two sets of cutoffs, with partial invariance where a step fails. Two further checks: whether the two groups answer alike before the training, and how far the waves are from invariance when nothing is held equal (alignment). Only under scalar invariance can latent means be compared over time, which the difference-in-differences models of Chapter 11 do. Feeds the measurement-invariance paragraph of the Results and the invariance table of the supplement.
source("R/packages.R")                  # all packages (Chapter 1)
source("R/settings.R")                  # waves, conditions, folders (Chapter 1)
df      <- readRDS("cache/df.rds")      # one row per questionnaire (Chapter 2)
df_wide <- readRDS("cache/df_wide.rds") # one row per person (Chapter 2)
item_names <- names(select(df, ListenOther1:CompetenceNonFrustrated4))
source("R/scales.R")                    # the 23 scales (Chapter 2)
source("R/measurement.R")               # models of the constructs (Chapter 6)

title: 7. Measurement invariance over time
text:
7.1 One model over four waves
How is invariance over time tested? The four waves come from the same persons, so they are not four independent groups: the test is one of longitudinal invariance, with the persons as the units (Widaman, Ferrer & Conger, 2010; Liu et al., 2017). Each model is therefore a longitudinal factor model on the wide data (one row per person): one latent factor per wave, the four factors correlated, and each item’s residual correlated with itself across the waves (autocorrelated residuals; Little, 2013). Persons who missed a wave keep their other answers (full-information maximum likelihood, robust standard errors).
Three nested levels add constraints step by step:

configural: the same items load on the factor at every wave; the first item is the marker (loading 1), all other loadings and all intercepts are free;
metric: each loading keeps one value over the four waves;
scalar: each intercept keeps one value over the four waves as well; the latent means are then free (T0 is the reference at 0), and only now are they comparable over time.

Constructs with two items are identified tau-equivalently: both items share one loading at every wave, and the factor variance is 1 at T0. For them the configural and the metric model are the same model, and only the scalar step tests anything.
The syntax of every model is written by one function:

# Longitudinal models: one latent factor per wave (Chapters 7 and 11)
#
# invariance_model() writes the lavaan syntax of the configural, metric or
# scalar model of a construct from R/measurement.R over the four waves;
# `free_loading` and `free_intercept` leave the loadings or intercepts of
# some items without a label (partial invariance), at every wave ("Agency2")
# or at one wave ("Agency2_T1").

waves <- paste0("T", 0:3)

# wide item names: Agency1 at T0 is Agency1_T0
at <- \(items, wave) paste0(items, "_", wave)

# the six pairs of waves: T0 and T1, T0 and T2, ..., T2 and T3
wave_pairs <- combn(waves, 2, simplify = FALSE)

invariance_model <- \(construct,
                      level = c("configural", "metric", "scalar"),
                      free_intercept = NULL,
                      free_loading = NULL,
                      tau_equivalent = TRUE) {
  level <- match.arg(level)
  items <- model_items[[construct]]
  pairs <- residual_pairs |> filter(construct == .env$construct)
  two_items <- length(items) == 2 && tau_equivalent
  is_free <- \(item, wave, free) item %in% free || at(item, wave) %in% free

  # loadings: two items share one label L at every wave (tau-equivalent,
  # factor variance 1 at T0); otherwise the first item is the marker, and
  # from the metric level on each loading keeps its label over the waves
  loading_label <- \(j, wave) {
    if (j == 1) return("1*")
    if (level == "configural" || is_free(items[j], wave, free_loading)) {
      return("")
    }
    str_c("lam", j, "*")
  }
  loadings <- if (two_items) {
    map_chr(waves, \(w) str_c("F_", w, " =~ NA*", at(items[1], w), " + ",
                              str_c("L*", at(items, w), collapse = " + ")))
  } else {
    map_chr(waves, \(w) str_c("F_", w, " =~ ",
                              str_c(map_chr(seq_along(items), loading_label, w),
                                    at(items, w), collapse = " + ")))
  }
  variance <- if (two_items) "F_T0 ~~ 1*F_T0" else character()

  # the four factors covary freely
  covariances <- map_chr(wave_pairs, \(p) str_c("F_", p[1], " ~~ F_", p[2]))

  # latent means: 0 at every wave; at the scalar level free from T1 on
  means <- if (level == "scalar") {
    c("F_T0 ~ 0*1", str_c("F_", waves[-1], " ~ 1"))
  } else {
    str_c("F_", waves, " ~ 0*1")
  }

  # intercepts at the scalar level: one label per item over the waves
  # (except those in `free_intercept`: partial invariance)
  intercepts <- if (level == "scalar") {
    imap(items, \(item, j) map_chr(waves, \(w) {
      label <- if (is_free(item, w, free_intercept)) "" else
        str_c("tau", j, "*")
      str_c(at(item, w), " ~ ", label, "1")
    })) |> unlist()
  } else {
    character()
  }

  # residual covariances within each wave (Chapter 6)
  within_waves <- map2(pairs$item_a, pairs$item_b, \(a, b)
    str_c(at(a, waves), " ~~ ", at(b, waves))) |> unlist()

  # autocorrelated residuals: each item with itself over all pairs of waves
  across_waves <- map(items, \(item) map_chr(wave_pairs, \(p)
    str_c(at(item, p[1]), " ~~ ", at(item, p[2])))) |> unlist()

  c(loadings, variance, covariances, means, intercepts, within_waves,
    across_waves) |>
    str_c(collapse = "\n")
}

# one sample, robust maximum likelihood, missing waves by full information
fit_longitudinal <- \(model, data = df_wide) {
  cfa(model, data = data, estimator = "MLR", missing = "fiml")
}

title: 7. Measurement invariance over time
text:
7.2 Fitting the models
Configural, metric and scalar, for all 22 constructs:

invariance_levels <- c("configural", "metric", "scalar")

invariance <- expand_grid(construct = names(model_items),
                          level     = invariance_levels) |>
  mutate(fit = map2(construct, level,
                    \(c, l) fit_longitudinal(invariance_model(c, l))),
         # admissible: no negative variance, no correlation beyond 1
         admissible = map_lgl(fit, \(f) suppressWarnings(
           lavInspect(f, "post.check"))))

title: 7. Measurement invariance over time
text:
7.3 Does each step hold?
Which constraints hold? A level holds when its fit worsens little compared with the level before, by the cutoffs Chen (2007) recommends for samples of more than 300: the robust CFI drops by no more than .010 and the robust RMSEA rises by no more than .015. The configural model needs an acceptable fit of its own (robust CFI of at least .90).

fit_indices <- \(fit) {
  fitMeasures(fit, c("chisq.scaled", "df", "cfi.robust", "rmsea.robust",
                     "srmr")) |>
    as.list() |>
    as_tibble() |>
    set_names(c("chisq", "df", "CFI", "RMSEA", "SRMR"))
}

# the change against the level before, and whether the level holds
steps <- \(indices) {
  indices |>
    mutate(delta_CFI   = CFI - lag(CFI),
           delta_RMSEA = RMSEA - lag(RMSEA),
           holds       = if_else(is.na(delta_CFI), CFI >= .90,
                                 delta_CFI >= -.010 & delta_RMSEA <= .015))
}

invariance_steps <- invariance |>
  mutate(indices = map(fit, fit_indices)) |>
  unnest(indices) |>
  select(-fit) |>
  group_by(construct) |>
  group_modify(\(levels, key) steps(levels)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(construct = factor(construct, levels = names(model_items))) |>
  arrange(construct)

invariance_steps |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))

In both, the residual of one item correlates with itself at another wave at about ±1, so the residual covariance matrix is not positive definite. The fit indices of these models are reported, but they rest on a boundary solution.
Do the verdicts hold under the cutoffs for small samples? The units of these models are the 451 persons, more than the 300 above which Chen’s cutoffs apply. Each wave, however, holds only the persons who answered it, so every constraint between two waves rests on fewer persons than the model as a whole, and Chen’s simulations, run with independent groups, do not tell on which side of 300 such a design lies. For samples of 300 or fewer, Chen (2007) reads a drop in CFI of at least .005, supplemented by a rise in RMSEA of at least .010 or in SRMR of at least .025 (loadings) or .005 (intercepts), as noninvariance. Here the CFI is the main criterion (Putnick & Bornstein, 2016): a step holds when the robust CFI drops by less than .005 and, in addition, the robust RMSEA or the SRMR stays within its limit.

Under the small-sample cutoffs only one step changes: the loadings of Autonomy Satisfaction cost .008 of CFI, more than the .005 allowed, although RMSEA and SRMR stay within their limits. 19 constructs keep full scalar invariance. Relatedness Non-Frustrated passes its scalar step narrowly (ΔCFI = -.0049), with the SRMR in place of the RMSEA, which rises by .011. title: 11. Latent difference-in-differences
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Estimates the training effects on the latent means of each construct: how much more the experimental group changes than the control group while it trains (January to March), and the mirrored effect when the control group trains (September to December). The models hold the measurement equal over the waves and over the two groups; Chapter 7 tests the first over all four waves and the second before the training, at T0. Besides the effects themselves, the chapter reports how the control group changes while it waits, the counts after a correction for multiple testing, a restricted model in which the latent means stay level outside the training, and the effects on the sample sets S0 to S9. Feeds the latent results of Hypotheses 1 to 3, the wait-list replication, the latent effect sizes and the sensitivity tables of the supplement.
source("R/packages.R")                  # all packages (Chapter 1)
source("R/settings.R")                  # waves, conditions, folders (Chapter 1)
df      <- readRDS("cache/df.rds")      # one row per questionnaire (Chapter 2)
df_wide <- readRDS("cache/df_wide.rds") # one row per person (Chapter 2)
item_names <- names(select(df, ListenOther1:CompetenceNonFrustrated4))
source("R/scales.R")                    # the 23 scales (Chapter 2)
source("R/measurement.R")               # models of the constructs (Chapter 6)
source("R/longitudinal_models.R")       # waves, at(), wave_pairs (Chapter 7)
invariance <- readRDS("cache/invariance.rds") # verdicts (Chapter 7)

title: 11. Latent difference-in-differences
text:
11.1 The model
How does a factor model estimate a difference-in-differences? Each construct gets one structured-means model in two groups, Control and Experimental, on the wide data (Seddig et al., 2022; Andersen & Seddig, 2026). Four parts make it a latent difference-in-differences:

Measurement held equal. Loadings and intercepts keep their labels over the four waves and, because lavaan applies a label in every group, over the two groups. Chapter 7 tests the equality over the waves (7.3) and, before the training, over the groups (7.6); there the χ² test finds different loadings for Rogerian Schema and Tolerance Diversity and different intercepts for Paradox Mindset and Empowerment. The first item’s intercept is fixed at 0, so the latent means lie on that item’s scale from 0 to 10. Two-item constructs are again tau-equivalent, with factor variances of 1; their means are in latent standard deviations.
Eight free latent means, one per group and wave.
The backbone of Chapter 7: correlated factors, residual covariances within a wave and autocorrelated residuals over the waves. Age (centred) and sex enter as covariates, with one path per group.
Every contrast is a parameter. For each of the six windows between two waves: the change in the experimental group (EG), in the control group (CG) and their difference (DiD, positive when the experimental group gains more). Standard errors come from the delta method.

The wait-list design adds a test: if the training works the same in both groups, the effect while the experimental group trains (T0 to T1) and the mirrored effect while the control group trains (T2 to T3) cancel out. A replication test near 0 supports this; it is a significance test, not an equivalence test.

# Latent difference-in-differences (Chapter 11): a structured-means model of
# one construct in two groups over the four waves (Seddig et al., 2022).
# Needs R/measurement.R and R/longitudinal_models.R (waves, at(), wave_pairs).

# the six windows between two waves
windows <- c(
  T01 = "T0 to T1, January to March: the experimental group trains",
  T02 = "T0 to T2, January to September: durability",
  T03 = "T0 to T3, January to December: the full year",
  T12 = "T1 to T2, March to September: maintenance",
  T13 = "T1 to T3, March to December: maintenance and control training",
  T23 = "T2 to T3, September to December: the control group trains"
)

# a window's name from its two waves: T0 and T1 -> T01
window_of <- \(pair) str_c("T", str_sub(pair[1], 2), str_sub(pair[2], 2))

smm_model <- \(construct, covariates = c("age_c", "female")) {
  items <- model_items[[construct]]
  pairs <- residual_pairs |> filter(construct == .env$construct)
  two_items <- length(items) == 2

  # loadings equal over the waves and, since labels hold in every group,
  # over the two groups; two items share one label L (tau-equivalent, factor
  # variances 1)
  labels <- c("1*", paste0("lam", seq_along(items)[-1], "*"))
  loadings <- if (two_items) {
    map_chr(waves, \(w) str_c("F_", w, " =~ NA*", at(items[1], w), " + ",
                              str_c("L*", at(items, w), collapse = " + ")))
  } else {
    map_chr(waves, \(w) str_c("F_", w, " =~ ",
                              str_c(labels, at(items, w), collapse = " + ")))
  }
  variances <- if (two_items) str_c("F_", waves, " ~~ 1*F_", waves) else
    character()
  covariances <- map_chr(wave_pairs, \(p) str_c("F_", p[1], " ~~ F_", p[2]))

  # intercepts equal over waves and groups; the first item's intercept is 0,
  # so that the latent means lie on its scale from 0 to 10
  intercepts <- imap(items, \(item, j) {
    label <- if (j == 1) "0*" else str_c("tau", j, "*")
    str_c(at(item, waves), " ~ ", label, "1")
  }) |> unlist()

  # eight free latent means: Control and Experimental at each wave
  means <- str_c("F_", waves, " ~ c(m_con_", waves, ", m_exp_", waves, ")*1")

  # residual covariances within each wave, autocorrelated residuals over
  # the waves (as in Chapter 7)
  within_waves <- map2(pairs$item_a, pairs$item_b, \(a, b)
    str_c(at(a, waves), " ~~ ", at(b, waves))) |> unlist()
  across_waves <- map(items, \(item) map_chr(wave_pairs, \(p)
    str_c(at(item, p[1]), " ~~ ", at(item, p[2])))) |> unlist()

  # covariates: one path per group (g1 Control, g2 Experimental), equal over
  # the waves, and the difference between the groups
  gammas <- map(covariates, \(cv)
    str_c("F_", waves, " ~ c(g1_", cv, ", g2_", cv, ")*", cv)) |> unlist()
  gamma_differences <- str_c("delta_gamma_", covariates, " := g2_",
                             covariates, " - g1_", covariates)

  # per window: change in each group (EG, CG) and their difference (DiD,
  # positive when the experimental group gains more)
  change <- \(group, p) str_c("(m_", group, "_", p[2], " - m_", group, "_",
                              p[1], ")")
  contrasts <- map(wave_pairs, \(p) c(
    str_c("EG_", window_of(p), " := ", change("exp", p)),
    str_c("CG_", window_of(p), " := ", change("con", p)),
    str_c("DiD_", window_of(p), " := ", change("exp", p), " - ",
          change("con", p))
  )) |> unlist()

  # wait-list replication: the two training effects cancel out
  replication <- str_c(
    "Replication_test := ",
    change("exp", c("T0", "T1")), " - ", change("con", c("T0", "T1")), " + ",
    change("exp", c("T2", "T3")), " - ", change("con", c("T2", "T3"))
  )

  # the order matters: for Women Attitude, whose solution lies at a
  # boundary, it decides which of two optima the estimation reaches
  c(loadings, intercepts, variances, covariances, means, within_waves,
    across_waves, gammas, gamma_differences, contrasts, replication) |>
    str_c(collapse = "\n")
}

# two groups, robust maximum likelihood, missing waves by full information
fit_smm <- \(model, data = df_wide) {
  sem(model, data = data, group = "condition", estimator = "MLR",
      missing = "fiml")
}

11.2 Fitting the models
All 22 constructs, also those without scalar invariance (their contrasts are marked below):

  mutate(fit        = map(construct, \(c) fit_smm(smm_model(c))),
         admissible = map_lgl(fit, \(f) suppressWarnings(
           lavInspect(f, "post.check"))),
         scalar     = construct %in% invariance$scalar_invariant)

Who enters the models? Age and sex are covariates, fixed as observed; persons without either drop out:

Every model uses the same 237 control and 191 experimental participants; the 23 persons without age or sex are not part of the latent comparisons.
Are the solutions admissible? A solution is not admissible when a variance is negative or a correlation lies beyond ±1. For each model that is not, the estimates at fault:

# negative variances and correlations beyond ±1, per group
boundary_estimates <- \(fit) {
  groups <- lavInspect(fit, "group.label")
  negative <- parameterEstimates(fit) |>
    filter(op == "~~", lhs == rhs, est < 0) |>
    transmute(group, problem = "negative variance", parameter = lhs,
              value = est)
  beyond <- standardizedSolution(fit) |>
    filter(op == "~~", lhs != rhs, abs(est.std) > 1) |>
    transmute(group, problem = "correlation beyond 1",
              parameter = str_c(lhs, " with ", rhs), value = est.std)
  found <- bind_rows(negative, beyond) |>
    mutate(group = groups[group], value = round(value, 2))
  if (nrow(found) > 0) return(found)
  tibble(group = NA_character_, problem = "covariances not positive definite",
         parameter = NA_character_, value = NA_real_)
}

smm_boundary <- smm |>
  filter(!admissible) |>
  mutate(estimates = map(fit, boundary_estimates)) |>
  select(construct, scalar, estimates) |>
  unnest(estimates)

Which effects are significant? Among the scalar-invariant constructs (Chapter 7):

scalar_effects <- training_effects |> filter(scalar)
positive_T01 <- scalar_effects |> filter(DiD_T01_pvalue < .05, DiD_T01_est > 0)
negative_T23 <- scalar_effects |> filter(DiD_T23_pvalue < .05, DiD_T23_est < 0)
against_T01  <- scalar_effects |> filter(DiD_T01_pvalue < .05, DiD_T01_est < 0)

Of the 20 scalar-invariant constructs, 8 show a significant positive DiD while the experimental group trains: Others Listen to Me, Positivity Resonance, Belongingness, Rogerian Schema, Paradox Mindset, Autonomy Satisfaction, Relatedness Satisfaction, and Competence Satisfaction. 4 show the mirrored negative DiD while the control group trains: Others Listen to Me, Kama Muta, Belongingness, and Flourishing. One construct moves against the training in the first window: No Alienation (DiD = -0.28, p = .017).
Do the counts hold with a correction for multiple testing? Each window tests 20 constructs. The p-values adjusted by Benjamini and Hochberg (1995), within each window, hold the expected share of false discoveries at 5 %:

  mutate(DiD_T01_p_BH = p.adjust(DiD_T01_pvalue, method = "BH"),

title: 11. Latent difference-in-differences
text:
11.7 Latent effect sizes
How large are the effects in standard deviations? The DiD divided by the latent standard deviation at T0, pooled over the two groups (Hancock, 2001). For two-item constructs the residual factor variance is 1; the covariates add a small explained share, so their pooled SD lies just above 1. The two training windows also carry Cohen’s (1988) labels: below .2 negligible, from .2 small, from .5 medium, from .8 large.

# pooled latent SD at T0 over the two groups
pooled_sd_T0 <- \(fit) {
  lavInspect(fit, "cov.lv") |>
    map_dbl(\(group) group["F_T0", "F_T0"]) |>
    mean() |>
    sqrt()
}

latent_d <- smm |>
  mutate(sd_T0 = map_dbl(fit, pooled_sd_T0)) |>
  select(construct, scalar, sd_T0) |>
  left_join(smm_estimates |>
              filter(str_starts(label, "DiD_")) |>
              select(construct, label, est),
            by = "construct") |>
  mutate(d = est / sd_T0, window = str_remove(label, "^DiD_")) |>
  select(construct, scalar, window, d) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = window, values_from = d)

# Cohen's (1988) benchmarks for |d|
cohen <- \(d) cut(abs(d), breaks = c(0, .2, .5, .8, Inf), right = FALSE,
                  labels = c("negligible", "small", "medium", "large"))

latent_d |>
  mutate(T01_size = cohen(T01), T23_size = cohen(T23)) |>
  relocate(T01_size, .after = T01) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))

title: 9. Means and Δd
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Describes the scale scores by condition and wave and measures the change of each group in standard deviations (repeated-measures d). The difference between the groups, Δd, is the descriptive counterpart of the difference-in-differences: while the experimental group trains (T0 to T1) and while the control group trains (T2 to T3). The Δd are shown with their intervals, recomputed with the standard deviation of all questionnaires before the window, and corrected for testing 23 scales; a dropout analysis asks whether the later gains come from who stays in the study. Feeds the table and figures of means and effect sizes of the Results; Chapter 14 repeats the Δd on the sample sets S0 to S9.
source("R/packages.R")                  # all packages (Chapter 1)
source("R/settings.R")                  # waves, conditions, folders (Chapter 1)

title: 9. Means and Δd
text:
9.2 Repeated-measures d
How large is the change of each group? For each group and window, d is the mean change divided by the standard deviation before the window (Morris & DeShon, 2002); Δd is the d of the experimental group minus the d of the control group, tested with a z-test. Change, standard deviation and standard error all rest on the persons who answered at both waves of the window.

# Repeated-measures effect sizes (Chapters 9 and 14)
#
# d_rm(): the change of one group in one window, in standard deviations
# before the window (Morris & DeShon, 2002). Change, SD and standard error
# all come from the persons who answered at both waves.
# delta_d(): the difference experimental minus control, with a z-test.
# With sd_pre = "all", d is divided by the SD of every questionnaire of the
# group at the first wave, not only of the pairs; the standard error stays
# that of the pairs.

d_rm <- \(data, outcome, pre, post, group, sd_pre = "pairs") {
  waves <- data |>
    filter(condition == group, Occasion %in% c(pre, post)) |>
    select(id, Occasion, value = all_of(outcome))
  pairs <- waves |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = Occasion, values_from = value) |>
    drop_na()
  change <- mean(pairs[[post]] - pairs[[pre]])
  d <- change / sd(pairs[[pre]])
  r <- cor(pairs[[pre]], pairs[[post]])
  n <- nrow(pairs)
  se <- sqrt(2 * (1 - r) / n + d^2 / (2 * n))
  sd_all <- sd(waves$value[waves$Occasion == pre], na.rm = TRUE)
  tibble(d = if (sd_pre == "all") change / sd_all else d, se = se, n = n)
}

delta_d <- \(data, pre, post, outcomes, sd_pre = "pairs") {
  map(outcomes, \(outcome) {
    eg <- d_rm(data, outcome, pre, post, "Experimental", sd_pre)
    cg <- d_rm(data, outcome, pre, post, "Control", sd_pre)
    tibble(outcome = outcome,
           d_EG = eg$d, n_EG = eg$n, d_CG = cg$d, n_CG = cg$n,
           delta_d = eg$d - cg$d, se = sqrt(eg$se^2 + cg$se^2))
  }) |>
    list_rbind() |>
    mutate(z = delta_d / se, p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(z)))
}

Four windows: while the experimental group trains (T0 to T1), its durability (T0 to T2, T0 to T3), and while the control group trains (T2 to T3), where a negative Δd means the control group gains more.

effect_windows <- tribble(
  ~pre, ~post, ~window,
  "T0", "T1",  "T0 to T1: the experimental group trains",
  "T0", "T2",  "T0 to T2: durability until September",
  "T0", "T3",  "T0 to T3: the full year",
  "T2", "T3",  "T2 to T3: the control group trains"
)

effects <- effect_windows |>
  mutate(table = map2(pre, post, \(a, b) delta_d(df, a, b, outcomes))) |>
  unnest(table)
