title: 10. Multilevel models
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



The preregistered test of the training effects: one multilevel model per outcome with the interaction of wave and condition, questionnaires nested in persons nested in municipalities, and the same models with the trainers as a further level. Two further models replicate the effect when the control group trains, random slopes ask whether the change differs between trainers, municipalities and persons, also within each condition, and equivalence tests check the claims that the groups do not differ at baseline and after both trainings. One-sided tests and a correction for testing many outcomes show how much the counts of significant effects depend on these choices. Feeds the preregistered results of Hypotheses 1 to 3.
source("R/packages.R")                  # all packages (Chapter 1)
source("R/settings.R")                  # waves, conditions, folders (Chapter 1)
df      <- readRDS("cache/df.rds")      # one row per questionnaire (Chapter 2)
df_wide <- readRDS("cache/df_wide.rds") # one row per person (Chapter 2)
item_names <- names(select(df, ListenOther1:CompetenceNonFrustrated4))
source("R/scales.R")                    # the 23 scales (Chapter 2)
The outcomes are the 23 scale scores and the three hypothesis composites (Chapter 2). Two small helpers fit a model for any outcome and return its fixed effects with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom (lmerTest):
composites <- c("H1_ListeningTogetherness", "H2_CognitiveComplexity",
                "H3_Wellbeing")
outcomes   <- c(scales$scale, composites)

# readable names of the outcomes, for the text
composite_labels <- c(H1_ListeningTogetherness = "Listening and Togetherness",
                      H2_CognitiveComplexity   = "Cognitive Complexity",
                      H3_Wellbeing             = "Well-being")
label_of <- \(outcome) {
  coalesce(scales$label[match(outcome, scales$scale)],
           unname(composite_labels[outcome]))
}

# a multilevel model of one outcome: "outcome ~ " and the right-hand side
# (further arguments, such as the optimizer, go to lmer())
mlm <- \(outcome, rhs, data = df, REML = TRUE, ...) {
  lmer(as.formula(str_c(outcome, " ~ ", rhs)), data = data, REML = REML, ...)
}

# the fixed effects of a model, with Satterthwaite df and p
fixed <- \(fit) {
  tidy(fit, effects = "fixed") |>
    select(term, b = estimate, se = std.error, df, p = p.value)
}

title: 10. Multilevel models
text:
10.1 Random structure
Is the municipality a level of its own? The null model of each outcome with persons nested in municipalities, against persons alone, compared by AIC:

random_structure <- tibble(outcome = outcomes) |>
  mutate(null_nested = map(outcome, \(o) mlm(o, "1 + (1 | Municipality/id)")),
         null_person = map(outcome, \(o) mlm(o, "1 + (1 | id)")),
         AIC_nested  = map_dbl(null_nested, AIC),
         AIC_person  = map_dbl(null_person, AIC),
         better      = if_else(AIC_nested <= AIC_person,
                               "Municipality/id", "id"))

AIC prefers persons alone for 4 outcomes (Positivity Resonance, Belongingness, Rogerian Schema, and Relatedness Satisfaction). All models keep the municipality level nevertheless: the conditions were assigned by municipality, so the design calls for it, whatever its share of variance.
How is the variance shared? From the nested null models: the share of municipalities, of persons within municipalities, and of questionnaires within persons (the residual):

variance_shares <- \(fit) {
  as_tibble(VarCorr(fit)) |>
    transmute(level = case_match(grp, "id:Municipality" ~ "person",
                                 "Municipality" ~ "municipality",
                                 "Residual" ~ "residual"),
              share = vcov / sum(vcov)) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = level, values_from = share)
}

random_structure |>
  mutate(shares = map(null_nested, variance_shares)) |>
  select(outcome, shares) |>
  unnest(shares) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))

title: 10. Multilevel models
text:
10.2 The preregistered models
Does the experimental group change more? For each outcome: outcome ~ Occasion * condition + (1 | Municipality/id), fitted by REML. Each interaction term compares the change from T0 to that wave between the groups (positive: the experimental group changes more).

preregistered <- tibble(outcome = outcomes) |>
  mutate(fit = map(outcome, \(o)
    mlm(o, "Occasion * condition + (1 | Municipality/id)")))

interactions <- preregistered |>
  mutate(effects = map(fit, fixed)) |>
  select(outcome, effects) |>
  unnest(effects) |>
  filter(str_detect(term, ":")) |>
  mutate(wave = str_extract(term, "T[1-3]"))

interactions |>
  select(outcome, wave, b, se, p) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = wave, values_from = c(b, se, p),
              names_glue = "{wave}_{.value}") |>
  select(outcome, starts_with("T1"), starts_with("T2"), starts_with("T3")) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))

At T1, 10 scales show a significant interaction in favour of the experimental group, led by Others Listen to Me, Paradox Mindset, and I Listen (b = 0.82, 0.71, 0.60); No Alienation again moves against the training (b = -0.76). By T2, 5 interactions remain significant: the advantage fades before the control group trains. At T3, 2 interactions are significantly negative, as the freshly trained control group catches up. Of the composites, only Cognitive Complexity (H2) shows a significant interaction at T1 (b = 0.31).
Does the result hold with a trainer level? The preregistration names the trainers, together with their municipalities, as the random factor. Each trainer trained one municipality in each condition, so the municipalities are nested in the trainers. The same models with persons in municipalities in trainers, fitted with the bobyqa optimizer (with the default one, three of them stop short of convergence), against the models above by AIC:

with_trainer <- tibble(outcome = outcomes) |>
  mutate(fit = map(outcome, \(o)
    mlm(o, "Occasion * condition + (1 | trainedBy/Municipality/id)",
        control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))))

# the share of the variance that lies between trainers
trainer_share <- \(fit) {
  vc <- as_tibble(VarCorr(fit))
  sum(vc$vcov[vc$grp == "trainedBy"]) / sum(vc$vcov)
}

trainer_comparison <- preregistered |>
  transmute(outcome, AIC_municipality = map_dbl(fit, AIC)) |>
  left_join(with_trainer |>
              transmute(outcome, AIC_trainer = map_dbl(fit, AIC),
                        trainer_share = map_dbl(fit, trainer_share)),
            by = "outcome")

trainer_comparison |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("AIC"), \(x) round(x, 1)),
         trainer_share = round(trainer_share, 3))

title: 10. Multilevel models
text:
10.5 Random slopes
Does the change differ between trainers and municipalities? Helmert contrasts code time (T0 against later waves; T3 against earlier waves, Chapter 2). A model with random slopes of both contrasts at the trainer and municipality levels is compared with random intercepts only, by a likelihood-ratio test on maximum-likelihood fits:

slopes <- tibble(outcome = composites) |>
  mutate(intercepts = map(outcome, \(o) mlm(o,
           "TF_helmert + TS_helmert + (1 | trainedBy/Municipality) + (1 | id)",
           REML = FALSE)),
         slopes = map(outcome, \(o) mlm(o,
           "TF_helmert + TS_helmert +
            (TF_helmert + TS_helmert | trainedBy/Municipality) + (1 | id)",
           REML = FALSE)),
         test = map2(intercepts, slopes, \(a, b) anova(a, b)[2, ])) |>
  select(outcome, test) |>
  unnest(test) |>
  select(outcome, chisq = Chisq, df = Df, p = `Pr(>Chisq)`)

  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))

None of the three composites shows significant slope variance across trainers and municipalities. Condition varies between municipalities and is not in these models, so slope variance at the municipality level would partly express the training effect itself rather than differences between trainers.
Does the change vary within each condition? Within one condition every municipality had the same schedule, so slope variance there is free of the training effect. For all 26 outcomes and each condition separately, four likelihood-ratio tests on maximum-likelihood fits:

random slopes of both contrasts across municipalities, against random intercepts. Within one condition each trainer worked in exactly one municipality, so trainers and municipalities are the same ten groups and one level stands for both;
a random slope across persons, for each contrast on its own: both at once would need more random effects than there are questionnaires;
a fixed interaction of municipality and pre/post in the arm’s own training window (T0 to T1 in the experimental group, T2 to T3 in the control group): do the ten municipalities gain differently from their training?

Slope variances near zero make single optimizers stop at different points, so every model is fitted with three and the best fit is kept. The 208 tests take more than a minute and run as a script:

# Random slopes within each condition (Chapter 10.5): for the 23 scales and
# the three composites, in each condition separately, whether the change
# varies between municipalities and between persons, and whether the
# municipalities change differently in their own training window.
# Likelihood-ratio tests on maximum-likelihood fits (about 1.5 minutes).
# Run from swt-website/ after Chapter 2:  Rscript scripts/slopes_within.R

source("R/packages.R")
source("R/settings.R")
df <- readRDS("cache/df.rds")      # one row per questionnaire (Chapter 2)
item_names <- names(select(df, ListenOther1:CompetenceNonFrustrated4))
source("R/scales.R")               # the 23 scales (Chapter 2)

outcomes <- c(scales$scale, "H1_ListeningTogetherness",
              "H2_CognitiveComplexity", "H3_Wellbeing")
time     <- "TF_helmert + TS_helmert"   # the two time contrasts (Chapter 2)

# each arm's own training window: T0 to T1 (experimental), T2 to T3 (control)
training_window <- list(Experimental = c("T0", "T1"),
                        Control      = c("T2", "T3"))

# a maximum-likelihood fit with three optimizers, keeping the best: with slope
# variances near zero, single optimizers stop at different points
ml_fit <- \(formula, data) {
  fits <- map(c("bobyqa", "Nelder_Mead", "nloptwrap"), \(optimizer)
    suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
      lmer(as.formula(formula), data = data, REML = FALSE,
           control = lmerControl(optimizer = optimizer)))))
  fits[[which.max(map_dbl(fits, logLik))]]
}

# likelihood-ratio test of a model against the same model with more terms
lr_test <- \(data, outcome, base, extended) {
  m0 <- ml_fit(str_c(outcome, " ~ ", base), data)
  m1 <- ml_fit(str_c(outcome, " ~ ", extended), data)
  chisq <- max(2 * (as.numeric(logLik(m1)) - as.numeric(logLik(m0))), 0)
  df    <- attr(logLik(m1), "df") - attr(logLik(m0), "df")
  tibble(chisq = chisq, df = df, p = pchisq(chisq, df, lower.tail = FALSE))
}

# the four tests of one outcome in one condition
within_condition <- \(outcome, group) {
  data <- df |>
    filter(condition == group) |>
    drop_na(all_of(outcome))
  window <- training_window[[group]]
  in_window <- data |>
    filter(Occasion %in% window) |>
    mutate(post = as.integer(Occasion == window[2]))
  bind_rows(
    "slopes, municipalities" = lr_test(data, outcome,
      str_c(time, " + (1 | Municipality) + (1 | id)"),
      str_c(time, " + (", time, " | Municipality) + (1 | id)")),
    "slope T0 vs. later, persons" = lr_test(data, outcome,
      str_c(time, " + (1 | id)"),
      str_c(time, " + (1 + TF_helmert | id)")),
    "slope T3 vs. earlier, persons" = lr_test(data, outcome,
      str_c(time, " + (1 | id)"),
      str_c(time, " + (1 + TS_helmert | id)")),
    "municipality x pre/post" = lr_test(in_window, outcome,
      "Municipality + post + (1 | id)",
      "Municipality * post + (1 | id)"),
    .id = "test")
}

slopes_within <- expand_grid(outcome   = outcomes,
                             condition = c("Experimental", "Control")) |>
  mutate(tests = map2(outcome, condition, within_condition)) |>
  unnest(tests)

Between municipalities the change hardly varies within a condition: 4 of the 52 slope tests are significant, about as many as chance alone gives at α = .05 (2.6), and in no outcome do the ten municipalities of an arm gain differently from their training (smallest p = .058). title: 10. Multilevel models
text:
10.6 Equivalence tests
Do the groups really not differ? Two claims of the preregistration are claims of absence: the groups do not differ at baseline (condition at T0), and they no longer differ after both have trained (condition × T3). A non-significant test does not show absence; two one-sided tests (TOST) do, against a smallest effect of interest of Δd = ±0.20. Each coefficient of the preregistered models (10.2) is divided by the standard deviation of the outcome at T0. Equivalence holds when the 90 % confidence interval lies within ±0.20.

sesoi <- .20

# the TOST of one coefficient, in units of the SD at T0
tost <- \(fit, term, sd_T0) {
  fixed(fit) |>
    filter(term == .env$term) |>
    transmute(term,
              delta_d = b / sd_T0,
              se_d    = se / sd_T0,
              ci_low  = delta_d - qt(.95, df) * se_d,
              ci_high = delta_d + qt(.95, df) * se_d,
              p_tost  = pmax(pt((delta_d + sesoi) / se_d, df,
                                lower.tail = FALSE),
                             pt((delta_d - sesoi) / se_d, df)),
              p_two_sided = p)
}

# the verdict of the TOST, next to the two-sided test
verdict_of <- \(p_tost, p_two_sided) case_when(
  p_tost < .05 & p_two_sided >= .05 ~ "equivalent",
  p_tost < .05                      ~ "different but trivially small",
  p_two_sided < .05                 ~ "different",
  .default                          = "inconclusive"
)

# both claims for the models in `fit`, in units of the SD at T0
claims <- \(models) {
  models |>
    mutate(sd_T0 = map_dbl(outcome, \(o) sd(df[[o]][df$Occasion == "T0"],
                                            na.rm = TRUE))) |>
    mutate(after_both = pmap(list(fit, "OccasionT3:conditionExperimental",
                                  sd_T0), tost),
           baseline   = pmap(list(fit, "conditionExperimental", sd_T0),
                             tost)) |>
    select(-c(fit, sd_T0)) |>
    pivot_longer(c(after_both, baseline), names_to = "claim",
                 values_to = "test") |>
    unnest(test) |>
    mutate(verdict = verdict_of(p_tost, p_two_sided))
}

equivalence <- claims(preregistered)

equivalence |>
  select(outcome, claim, delta_d, ci_low, ci_high, p_tost, p_two_sided,
         verdict) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))

No claim of absence can be shown as equivalence: the 90 % intervals are about 0.43 units of Δd wide, wider than the band of ±0.20 itself. Most tests are inconclusive; the groups differ for Kama Muta and Intellectual Humility after both trainings and for Others Listen to Me and Competence Satisfaction at baseline. The intervals, not the verdicts, are the result to report.
Does the verdict depend on the random structure? Another rule gives each outcome the richest structure whose variances all lie above zero: persons in municipalities in trainers, else persons in municipalities, else persons alone (fitted with bobyqa). The same tests with that structure:

structures <- c("(1 | trainedBy/Municipality/id)", "(1 | Municipality/id)",
                "(1 | id)")

# the richest structure whose variances all lie above zero
richest <- \(outcome) {
  fits <- map(structures, \(s)
    mlm(outcome, str_c("Occasion * condition + ", s),
        control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")))
  first <- detect_index(fits, \(f) all(as_tibble(VarCorr(f))$vcov >= 1e-8))
  tibble(structure = structures[first], fit = fits[first])
}

equivalence_richest <- tibble(outcome = outcomes) |>
  mutate(models = map(outcome, richest)) |>
  unnest(models) |>
  claims()

title: 13. Movers
section: 13.4 Each group in its own training window
text:
13.4 Each group in its own training window
Does the trained group improve more often? On the 127 persons with all four waves, so that both windows rest on the same persons: the share who improved (strict criterion) in each condition, compared by a two-proportion test.

improvement <- \(score, pre, post) {
  rates <- change_between(complete, score, pre, post) |>
    summarise(persons  = n(),
              improved = sum(change > 0),
              declined = sum(change < 0),
              .by = condition) |>
    arrange(condition) |>
    mutate(improved_percent = round(100 * improved / persons, 1))
  test <- prop.test(rates$improved, rates$persons, correct = FALSE)
  rates |>
    mutate(chisq = unname(test$statistic), p = test$p.value)
}

windows <- tribble(
  ~score,               ~pre, ~post,
  "ToleranceDiversity", "T0", "T1",
  "ToleranceDiversity", "T2", "T3",
  "womenAttitude_full", "T0", "T1",
  "womenAttitude_full", "T2", "T3"
)

window_rates <- windows |>
  mutate(rates = pmap(list(score, pre, post), improvement)) |>
  unnest(rates)

window_rates |>
  mutate(across(c(chisq, p), \(x) round(x, 3)))

title: 14. Robustness across sample sets
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Repeats the training effects on the sample sets S0 to S9: the repeated-measures Δd of Chapter 9 and the preregistered multilevel models of Chapter 10, once for each way of choosing persons and questionnaires, and the Δd also with the standard deviation of all questionnaires before the window. An effect that holds across the sets does not depend on who answered when or on careless answering; the latent effects across the same sets follow in Chapter 11.9. Feeds the robustness table of the supplement.

title: 14. Robustness across sample sets
text:
14.1 The sample sets
Which questionnaires does each set keep? S0 to S6 come from the waves a person answered (Chapter 3), S8 and S9 from the screening for careless answering (Chapter 4). S7, the set without the paper forms entered twice, is the analysis file itself (Chapter 1).

df <- df |>
  left_join(select(careless, id, Occasion, s8_no_careless,
                   s9_no_careless_strict),
            by = c("id", "Occasion"))

sample_sets <- tribble(
  ~set, ~flag,                   ~definition,
  "S0", NA,                      "all questionnaires",
  "S1", "s1_complete",           "persons with all four waves",
  "S2", "s2_no_singletons",      "persons with at least two waves",
  "S3", "s3_has_T0",             "persons with a January questionnaire",
  "S4", "s4_T0_plus_post",       "January and a wave after the own training",
  "S5", "s5_group_baseline",     "both waves around the own training",
  "S6", "s6_no_T0_dropouts",     "not January only",
  "S8", "s8_no_careless",        "without careless answering (lenient flag)",
  "S9", "s9_no_careless_strict", "without careless answering (strict flag)"
)

# the questionnaires of a set
set_data <- \(flag) if (is.na(flag)) df else filter(df, .data[[flag]])

sample_sets <- sample_sets |>
  mutate(data           = map(flag, set_data),
         questionnaires = map_int(data, nrow),

title: 14. Robustness across sample sets
text:
14.2 Δd of the composites
Does the descriptive effect hold in every set? The Δd of the three hypothesis composites (Chapter 9), in the four windows:

composites <- c("H1_ListeningTogetherness", "H2_CognitiveComplexity",
                "H3_Wellbeing")
windows <- tribble(
  ~pre, ~post,
  "T0", "T1",
  "T0", "T2",
  "T0", "T3",
  "T2", "T3"
)

# the Δd of `outcomes` in every set and window (sd_pre as in delta_d())
set_effects <- \(windows, outcomes, sd_pre = "pairs") {
  sample_sets |>
    select(set, data) |>
    cross_join(windows) |>
    mutate(table = pmap(list(data, pre, post), \(d, a, b)
      delta_d(d, a, b, outcomes, sd_pre))) |>
    select(set, pre, post, table) |>
    unnest(table) |>
    mutate(window = str_c(pre, " to ", post))
}

robust_delta_d <- set_effects(windows, composites)

robust_delta_d |>
  mutate(estimate = sprintf("%.2f (p = %.3f)", delta_d, p)) |>
  select(window, outcome, set, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = set, values_from = estimate)

title: 12. Serial mediation
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Tests the preregistered pathway of the training: training → listening and togetherness (H1) → cognitive complexity (H2) → well-being (H3), in four windows between two waves. Indirect effects carry bootstrap confidence intervals; cluster-robust and complete-case fits check them, and a model with latent blocks (structural after measurement) asks whether they hold when measurement error is modelled. Feeds the mediation results of the paper.
source("R/packages.R")                  # all packages (Chapter 1)
source("R/settings.R")                  # waves, conditions, folders (Chapter 1)
df      <- readRDS("cache/df.rds")      # one row per questionnaire (Chapter 2)
df_wide <- readRDS("cache/df_wide.rds") # one row per person (Chapter 2)
item_names <- names(select(df, ListenOther1:CompetenceNonFrustrated4))
source("R/scales.R")                    # the 23 scales (Chapter 2)

title: 12. Serial mediation
text:
12.1 The model
How does the training reach well-being? In each window, the composite scores at the end of the window are regressed in sequence: H1 on training, H2 on H1 and training, H3 on H2, H1 and training. All three regressions control for the three composites at the start of the window. The indirect effect on H3 splits into three paths: through H1 alone, through H2 alone, and through H1 and H2 in series. Within a wave, H1, H2 and H3 are measured at the same time; their order inside the wave is a theoretical assumption, not a feature of the design.

# Serial mediation (Chapter 12): training -> listening and togetherness (H1)
# -> cognitive complexity (H2) -> well-being (H3) in one window, controlling
# for the three composites at the start of the window

# the four windows and the group that trains in each
mediation_windows <- tribble(
  ~model, ~pre, ~post, ~treated,   ~reading,
  1,      "T0", "T1",  "train_eg", "the experimental group trains",
  2,      "T0", "T2",  "train_eg", "durability from baseline",
  3,      "T1", "T2",  "train_eg", "maintenance, no new training",
  4,      "T2", "T3",  "train_cg", "the control group trains (replication)"
)

# the wide names of the composites at a wave: T1_Hypothesis2_... and so on
composite_at <- \(wave) {
  str_c(wave, "_", c("Hypothesis1_ListeningTogetherness",
                     "Hypothesis2_CognitiveComplexity",
                     "Hypothesis3_Wellbeing"))
}

mediation_model <- \(pre, post, treated) {
  before   <- composite_at(pre)
  after    <- composite_at(post)
  controls <- str_c(before, collapse = " + ")
  c(
    # paths: a (training -> H1), b1 and b2 (-> H2), c1 to c3 (-> H3)
    str_c(after[1], " ~ A*", treated, " + ", controls),
    str_c(after[2], " ~ B1*", after[1], " + B2*", treated, " + ", controls),
    str_c(after[3], " ~ C1*", after[2], " + C2*", after[1], " + C3*",
          treated, " + ", controls),
    # the controls covary
    str_c(before[1], " ~~ ", before[2]),
    str_c(before[1], " ~~ ", before[3]),
    str_c(before[2], " ~~ ", before[3]),
    # effects on H2
    "indirectH2 := A*B1",
    "directH2 := B2",
    "totalH2 := B2 + A*B1",
    # effects on H3: via H1, via H2, via both in series
    "ind_LET := A*C2",
    "ind_CF := B2*C1",
    "ind_serial := A*B1*C1",
    "total_indirect := A*C2 + B2*C1 + A*B1*C1",
    "directH3 := C3",
    "totalH3 := C3 + A*C2 + B2*C1 + A*B1*C1"
  ) |>
    str_c(collapse = "\n")
}

# maximum likelihood with 1,000 bootstrap draws (seed as before); missing
# values by full information ("fiml") or complete cases ("listwise")
fit_mediation <- \(model, data, missing = "fiml") {
  set.seed(20260525)
  sem(model, data = data, estimator = "ML", se = "bootstrap",
      bootstrap = 1000, missing = missing)
}

title: 12. Serial mediation
text:
12.2 Estimation
How are the models fitted? By maximum likelihood with 1,000 bootstrap draws, once with full information (FIML, all persons) and once with complete cases only. The bootstraps take a few minutes and run in a script of their own; this chapter reads its results.

# Serial mediation: the bootstrapped fits of Chapter 12, four windows, full
# information and complete cases, 1,000 draws each (about 6 minutes)
# Run from swt-website/ after Chapter 2:  Rscript scripts/mediation_bootstrap.R

source("R/packages.R")
source("R/settings.R")
source("R/mediation_model.R")
df_wide <- readRDS("cache/df_wide.rds")   # one row per person (Chapter 2)

mediation <- mediation_windows |>
  mutate(syntax   = pmap_chr(list(pre, post, treated), mediation_model),
         fiml     = map(syntax, \(m) fit_mediation(m, df_wide)),
         listwise = map(syntax, \(m) fit_mediation(m, df_wide, "listwise")))

saveRDS(mediation, "cache/mediation_bootstrap.rds")


mediation <- readRDS("cache/mediation_bootstrap.rds")

The FIML fits include all 451 persons; those without any answer in a window carry no information on it and leave the estimates unchanged.
How many persons carry each window? Those with at least one of the six composites of the window, who inform the FIML estimates, and those with all six, on whom the complete-case fits rest:

persons <- mediation |>
  mutate(variables = map2(pre, post, \(a, b)
           c(composite_at(a), composite_at(b))),
         fiml      = map_int(fiml, \(f) lavInspect(f, "nobs")),
         answering = map_int(variables, \(v)
           sum(rowSums(!is.na(df_wide[v])) > 0)),
         complete  = map_int(listwise, \(f) lavInspect(f, "nobs"))) |>
  select(model, pre, post, fiml, answering, complete)

title: 12. Serial mediation
text:
12.3 Effects in each window
Which effects carry? Indirect, direct and total effects, unstandardized, with bias-corrected bootstrap intervals (FIML) and the p-value of a z-test on the bootstrap standard error:

effect_labels <- c(
  indirectH2     = "H2: indirect via H1 (a × b1)",
  directH2       = "H2: direct (b2)",
  totalH2        = "H2: total",
  ind_LET        = "H3: indirect via H1 (a × c2)",
  ind_CF         = "H3: indirect via H2 (b2 × c1)",
  ind_serial     = "H3: serial via H1 and H2 (a × b1 × c1)",
  total_indirect = "H3: total indirect",
  directH3       = "H3: direct (c3)",
  totalH3        = "H3: total"
)

defined_effects <- \(fit) {
  parameterEstimates(fit, boot.ci.type = "bca.simple") |>
    filter(op == ":=") |>
    transmute(effect = label, est, ci_low = ci.lower, ci_high = ci.upper,
              p = pvalue)
}

mediation_effects <- mediation |>
  mutate(effects = map(fiml, defined_effects)) |>
  select(model, reading, effects) |>
  unnest(effects) |>
  mutate(effect = factor(effect_labels[effect], levels = effect_labels))

mediation_effects |>
  mutate(estimate = sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", est, ci_low, ci_high),
         p = round(p, 3)) |>
  select(model, effect, estimate, p) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = c(estimate, p),
              names_glue = "model{model}_{.value}") |>
  arrange(effect)

Which test decides for an indirect effect? The z-test assumes that an estimate is normally distributed across samples. An indirect effect is a product of paths, and the distribution of a product is skewed, so the bootstrap interval, which follows the skew, is the standard test for indirect effects (MacKinnon et al., 2004; Preacher & Hayes, 2008). In 4 single paths the interval excludes 0 while the z-test does not reach p < .05. One is the serial path of Model 1 (p = .078): its 1000 bootstrap draws are skewed to the right (skewness 0.64), and only 2.0 % of them lie at or below 0. The interval follows this shape, the z-test does not. By the interval, the serial path is significant in Model 1. For the total indirect effects the two tests agree in every window.
While the experimental group trains (Model 1), the total indirect effect on well-being is 0.18 [0.08, 0.30], and the serial path through H1 and H2 is 0.021 [0.003, 0.051]. The direct path is small, negative and not significant (-0.08), and so is the total effect of the training on well-being (0.10 [-0.08, 0.27], p = .273). This is an indirect-only mediation (Zhao et al., 2010): the path from the training through listening and togetherness and cognitive complexity to well-being carries, but in this window the training does not change well-being significantly in total. The results therefore show an indirect effect, not an effect on well-being that runs entirely through the mediators. While the control group trains (Model 4), the indirect effects repeat (total indirect 0.23, serial 0.030, both intervals excluding 0), the direct path is again not significant, and here the total effect is (0.21, p = .025). Between the trainings (Models 2 and 3), the total indirect effects are small and their intervals include 0 (0.07 and 0.01); two single paths exclude 0 by a narrow margin, the serial path of Model 2 (0.031) and the path through H2 of Model 3, which runs against the training (-0.034). The mediating process runs within the training windows.

title: 12. Serial mediation
text:
12.6 Path diagrams
The two training windows at a glance: standardized paths (FIML), with stars for p < .05, .01 and .001.

stars <- \(p) case_when(p < .001 ~ "***", p < .01 ~ "**", p < .05 ~ "*",
                        .default = "")

# boxes: centre (x, y) and half width and height (w, h)
nodes <- tribble(
  ~node, ~x,  ~y, ~w,  ~h,  ~text,
  "T",   0,   0,  .35, .1,  "Training",
  "L",   1.3, 1,  .6,  .17, "Listening and\ntogetherness (H1)",
  "C",   3.7, 1,  .6,  .17, "Cognitive\ncomplexity (H2)",
  "W",   5,   0,  .5,  .1,  "Well-being (H3)"
)
paths <- tribble(
  ~label, ~from, ~to,
  "A",    "T",   "L",
  "B1",   "L",   "C",
  "B2",   "T",   "C",
  "C1",   "C",   "W",
  "C2",   "L",   "W",
  "C3",   "T",   "W"
)

diagram_data <- estimators |>
  filter(estimator == "fiml", model %in% c(1, 4), label %in% paths$label) |>
  left_join(paths, by = "label") |>
  left_join(select(nodes, from = node, x0 = x, y0 = y, w0 = w, h0 = h),
            by = "from") |>
  left_join(select(nodes, to = node, x1 = x, y1 = y, w1 = w, h1 = h),
            by = "to") |>
  mutate(text   = str_c(str_to_lower(label), " = ", sprintf("%.2f", beta),
                        stars(p)),
         window = if_else(model == 1, "Model 1: T0 to T1, experimental trains",
                          "Model 4: T2 to T3, control trains"),
         # arrows run from the edge of one box to the edge of the other:
         # the share of the line inside each box, plus a small margin
         inside0 = pmin(w0 / abs(x1 - x0), h0 / abs(y1 - y0)) + .03,
         inside1 = pmin(w1 / abs(x1 - x0), h1 / abs(y1 - y0)) + .03,
         xs = x0 + inside0 * (x1 - x0), ys = y0 + inside0 * (y1 - y0),
         xe = x1 - inside1 * (x1 - x0), ye = y1 - inside1 * (y1 - y0))

ggplot(diagram_data) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = xs, y = ys, xend = xe, yend = ye,
                   linewidth = p < .05),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm"), type = "closed"),
               colour = "grey35") +
  geom_label(aes(x = (xs + xe) / 2, y = (ys + ye) / 2, label = text),
             size = 3, label.size = 0, fill = "white") +
  geom_label(data = nodes, aes(x = x, y = y, label = text), size = 3.3,
             fontface = "bold", label.padding = unit(3, "mm")) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = .9, `FALSE` = .3),
                         guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~ window, ncol = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(add = .3)) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(add = .6)) +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", margin = margin(b = 6)))

title: 5. Reliability and baseline correlations
text:
5.1 Reliability of the scales
How consistent are the items of each scale? α for scales with at least two items, ω (one factor) for scales with at least three, at each wave. The items are those of the scores (Chapter 2): reverse-keyed items turned, and Women Attitude without its two items at the ceiling.

scored_items <- map(scale_items, \(items) setdiff(items, ceiling_items))

# alpha and omega of a set of items in the questionnaires of one wave
consistency <- \(items, wave) {
  answers <- df |> filter(Occasion == wave) |> select(all_of(items))
  alpha_of <- \(x) psych::alpha(x, warnings = FALSE)$total$raw_alpha
  tibble(k     = length(items),
         alpha = if (k >= 2) alpha_of(answers) else NA,
         omega = if (k >= 3) psych::omega(answers, nfactors = 1,
                                          plot = FALSE)$omega.tot else NA)
}

reliability <- expand_grid(scale = scales$scale, wave = levels(df$Occasion)) |>
  mutate(values = map2(scale, wave, \(s, w)
    consistency(scored_items[[s]], w))) |>
  unnest(values)

Five further composites over the scored items: need satisfaction and need non-frustration from self-determination theory (the three satisfaction and the three non-frustration scales of H3), the negatively worded items (the 22 reverse-keyed items, after turning), the positively worded items (all others) and all items together:

# the 22 reverse-keyed items of Chapter 2, under their analysis names
negative_items <- c(str_c("NoAlienation", 1:2), str_c("NoIsolation", 1:2),
                    str_c("Flourishing", 5:6), str_c("Rogerian", 7:9),
                    "ToleranceDiversity1",
                    list_c(scale_items[str_subset(scales$scale,
                                                  "NonFrustrated")]))
scored <- setdiff(item_names, ceiling_items)

cross_items <- list(
  NeedSatisfaction   = list_c(scale_items[c("AutonomySatisfaction",
                                            "RelatednessSatisfaction",
                                            "CompetenceSatisfaction")]),
  NeedNonFrustration = list_c(scale_items[str_subset(scales$scale,
                                                     "NonFrustrated")]),
  NegativeItems      = negative_items,
  PositiveItems      = setdiff(scored, negative_items),
  AllItems           = scored
)

cross_reliability <- expand_grid(composite = names(cross_items),
                                 wave = levels(df$Occasion)) |>
  mutate(values = map2(composite, wave, \(c, w)
    consistency(cross_items[[c]], w))) |>
  unnest(values)

cross_reliability |>
  select(composite, k, wave, alpha) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = wave, values_from = alpha) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))

title: 6. Measurement models per wave
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Fits a one-factor model to each of the 22 multi-item constructs. The January wave calibrates the models: where the full item set does not fit, items are dropped or residual covariances added, and the revised models are then refitted unchanged at the three later waves. The resulting item sets (R/measurement.R) are the measurement models of Chapters 7 and 11. Feeds the description of the measures and the supplementary fit tables.
source("R/packages.R")                  # all packages (Chapter 1)
source("R/settings.R")                  # waves, conditions, folders (Chapter 1)
df      <- readRDS("cache/df.rds")      # one row per questionnaire (Chapter 2)
df_wide <- readRDS("cache/df_wide.rds") # one row per person (Chapter 2)
item_names <- names(select(df, ListenOther1:CompetenceNonFrustrated4))
source("R/scales.R")                    # the 23 scales (Chapter 2)

title: 6. Measurement models per wave
section: 6.1 One factor per construct and wave
text:
6.1 One factor per construct and wave
How is each construct modelled? One latent factor on the construct’s items, in the questionnaires of one wave, by robust maximum likelihood (MLR) with missing answers by full information. Two-item constructs are identified tau-equivalently, with equal loadings and a factor variance of 1. Understood has a single item and stays a manifest score.
The final item sets and residual covariances:

# Measurement models of the 22 latent constructs, as Chapter 6 settles them
# at T0: the items each factor keeps and the residual covariances it needs.
# Understood has a single item and stays a manifest score.

model_items <- list(
  # Hypothesis 1: listening and togetherness
  ListenOther          = paste0("ListenOther", 1:2),
  ListenSelf           = paste0("ListenSelf", 1:2),
  KamaMuta             = paste0("KamaMuta", 1:2),
  Resonance            = paste0("Resonance", 1:8),
  Belongingness        = paste0("Belongingness", 1:3),
  NoAlienation         = paste0("NoAlienation", 1:2),
  NoIsolation          = paste0("NoIsolation", 1:2),
  # Hypothesis 2: cognitive complexity
  Rogerian             = paste0("Rogerian", c(1, 3:5)),       # 2, 6 to 9 out
  ParadoxMindset       = paste0("ParadoxMindset", 2:9),       # 1 out
  IntellectualHumility = paste0("IntellectualHumility", c(1, 3:6)), # 2 out
  ToleranceDiversity   = paste0("ToleranceDiversity", 2:5),   # 1 out
  womenAttitude        = paste0("womenAttitude", c(4, 5, 8, 9)), # 1-3, 6, 7 out
  # Hypothesis 3: well-being
  Flourishing          = paste0("Flourishing", 1:4),          # 5 to 7 out
  AutonomySatisfaction     = paste0("AutonomySatisfaction", 1:4),
  RelatednessSatisfaction  = paste0("RelatednessSatisfaction", 1:4),
  CompetenceSatisfaction   = paste0("CompetenceSatisfaction", 1:4),
  AutonomyNonFrustrated    = paste0("AutonomyNonFrustrated", 1:4),
  RelatednessNonFrustrated = paste0("RelatednessNonFrustrated", 1:4),
  CompetenceNonFrustrated  = paste0("CompetenceNonFrustrated", 1:4),
  Empowerment          = paste0("Empowerment", c(1, 3:5)),    # 2 out
  Agency               = paste0("Agency", 1:3),
  IntellectualCapital  = paste0("IntellectualCapital", 1:3)
)

# residual covariances within a wave: pairs of items with shared wording
residual_pairs <- tribble(
  ~construct,       ~item_a,           ~item_b,
  "Resonance",      "Resonance1",      "Resonance2",
  "Resonance",      "Resonance4",      "Resonance5",
  "ParadoxMindset", "ParadoxMindset4", "ParadoxMindset5",
  "ParadoxMindset", "ParadoxMindset2", "ParadoxMindset7",
  "womenAttitude",  "womenAttitude4",  "womenAttitude5",
  "Flourishing",    "Flourishing1",    "Flourishing2",
  "Empowerment",    "Empowerment4",    "Empowerment5"
)


# the lavaan syntax of one construct at one wave: its items and, if wanted,
# the residual covariances of R/measurement.R
wave_model <- \(construct, items = model_items[[construct]],
                residuals = TRUE) {
  pairs <- residual_pairs |> filter(construct == .env$construct)
  syntax <- if (length(items) == 2) {
    c(str_c("F =~ NA*", items[1], " + ", str_c("L*", items, collapse = " + ")),
      "F ~~ 1*F")
  } else {
    str_c("F =~ ", str_c(items, collapse = " + "))
  }
  if (residuals) syntax <- c(syntax, str_c(pairs$item_a, " ~~ ", pairs$item_b))
  str_c(syntax, collapse = "\n")
}

fit_wave <- \(model, wave) {
  cfa(model, data = filter(df, Occasion == wave), estimator = "MLR",
      missing = "fiml.x")
}

fit_indices <- \(fit) {
  fitMeasures(fit, c("chisq.scaled", "df", "cfi.robust", "rmsea.robust",
                     "srmr")) |>
    as.list() |>
    as_tibble() |>
    set_names(c("chisq", "df", "CFI", "RMSEA", "SRMR"))
}

title: 6. Measurement models per wave
text:
6.2 Calibration at T0
Which constructs need a revision? Eight of the 22. Each of them is shown on its own below: first the one-factor model on all its items, with its weakest standardized loadings and its largest modification indices (MI) for residual covariances; then what changes and why; then the fit before and after. The other 14 constructs keep all their items (their fit at every wave follows in Section 6.3).

# a one-factor model at T0 on some items of a construct (by number), with
# residual covariances between pairs of them
t0_model <- \(construct, items, residuals = list()) {
  item <- \(i) str_c(construct, i)
  c(str_c("F =~ ", str_c(item(items), collapse = " + ")),
    map_chr(residuals, \(pair) str_c(item(pair[1]), " ~~ ", item(pair[2])))) |>
    str_c(collapse = "\n") |>
    fit_wave("T0")
}

# the weakest standardized loadings and the largest MIs of a model
weakest_loadings <- \(fit, n = 3) {
  standardizedSolution(fit) |>
    filter(op == "=~") |>
    slice_min(est.std, n = n) |>
    transmute(item = rhs, loading = round(est.std, 2))
}
largest_mi <- \(fit, n = 3) {
  modindices(fit, sort. = TRUE) |>
    filter(op == "~~") |>
    slice_head(n = n) |>
    transmute(pair = str_c(lhs, " ~~ ", rhs), mi = round(mi))
}

# the MI of one residual covariance
mi_of <- \(fit, a, b) {
  modindices(fit) |>
    filter(op == "~~", (lhs == a & rhs == b) | (lhs == b & rhs == a)) |>
    transmute(pair = str_c(lhs, " ~~ ", rhs), mi = round(mi, 1))
}

# several models of one construct, side by side
compare_fit <- \(...) {
  list(...) |>
    map(fit_indices) |>
    list_rbind(names_to = "model") |>
    mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
}

How strong are the factors? Standardized loadings (lowest and highest), model-based reliability ω and the average variance extracted (AVE), per construct and wave:

factor_strength <- \(fit) {

         omega = as.numeric(compRelSEM(fit)),

title: 15. Item pruning
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



The preregistration allowed a psychometric study that would “discard unreliable and redundant items to create more parsimonious measures”. Part D carries it out after the fact, on the questionnaires answered before any training (T0). This chapter takes items out of the pool on three grounds before any network is estimated: answers at the ceiling, negative wording, and the block on attitudes toward women. It also shows that the negatively worded items hardly respond to the training. Feeds the pruning step of the psychometric supplement; Chapters 16 to 18 build on the remaining pool.
source("R/packages.R")                  # all packages (Chapter 1)

source("R/scales.R")                    # the 23 scales (Chapter 2)

title: 15. Item pruning
text:
15.3 Negative wording
Do the negatively worded items respond to the training? Negatively worded items tend to form communities of their own in a network, defined by the direction of the wording rather than by its content, and they invite more answering errors. If they also carried the training effect, dropping them would cost signal. The test is the first training window: how much does each item move from T0 to T1 in the experimental group, beyond the change in the control group?
The measure here is a difference-in-differences d per item: the change of each group’s mean from T0 to T1, divided by the standard deviation at T0 pooled over both groups, experimental minus control. Unlike the Δd of Chapter 9, the means use every questionnaire of a group and wave, not only persons who answered at both waves. The negatively worded items enter reverse-keyed (Chapter 2), so a positive d always means a move toward the desired pole.

item_effects <- item_did(df) |>
  mutate(wording = if_else(item %in% negative_items, "negative",
                           "positive"))

item_effects |>
  summarise(items      = n(),
            mean_d     = mean(d_did),
            median_d   = median(d_did),
            mean_abs_d = mean(abs(d_did)),
            mean_d_E   = mean(d_E),
            .by = wording) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))

title: 16. Exploratory graph analysis
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Exploratory graph analysis (EGA) estimates a network of the items and finds the communities of items that hang together. Starting from the pool of Chapter 15, the chapter keeps the items whose community holds across bootstrap samples, describes the hierarchical structure of these items at each wave, and bootstraps that structure. Feeds the item-selection and structure steps of the psychometric supplement; Chapter 17 prunes the stable items further.
source("R/packages.R")                  # all packages (Chapter 1)

df_wide <- readRDS("cache/df_wide.rds") # one row per person (Chapter 2)

title: 16. Exploratory graph analysis
text:
16.1 The method
How does EGA find communities? The graphical lasso turns the correlations of the items into a network of partial correlations: two items are linked only if they share something that the other items do not explain, and weak links are set to zero. A community detection algorithm then groups items that are densely linked with each other (Golino & Epskamp, 2017). The bootstrap repeats this on 500 samples drawn from a normal distribution with the observed correlations. An item’s stability is the share of samples in which it lands in the same community as in the observed data (Christensen & Golino, 2021).
The hierarchical version (hierEGA) adds a second level: it scores the persons on each community of items (lower order) and runs EGA on these scores, which yields factors of communities (higher order). The functions and settings:

# Exploratory graph analysis (Chapters 16 and 18). The network of the items
# comes from the graphical lasso on pairwise correlations ("auto": Pearson
# for items with eleven answer categories); walktrap finds its communities,
# louvain the two levels of the hierarchical solution. Bootstraps draw 500
# samples from a normal distribution with the observed correlations, with
# seed 42; each hierarchical solution has a seed of its own per wave.
# Louvain draws random numbers (also when EGA checks a sample for a single
# dimension), which parallel workers do not seed: the bootstraps run in one
# process (ncores = 1), so that they repeat exactly.

# the label of an item's scale (needs `scales`, Chapter 2)
scale_label <- \(item) {
  scales$label[match(str_remove(item, "[0-9]+$"), scales$scale)]
}

# the answers of one wave to some items
items_at <- \(data, wave, items) {
  data |>
    filter(Occasion == wave) |>
    select(all_of(items))
}

# a bootstrap of the network and its communities
boot_ega <- \(items) {
  set.seed(42)
  bootEGA(items, iter = 500, type = "parametric", corr = "auto",
          model = "glasso", algorithm = "walktrap", na.data = "pairwise",
          seed = 42, ncores = 1, verbose = FALSE, plot.itemStability = FALSE)
}

# how often each item falls into its own community across the bootstrap
# samples; community = the community in the observed data
item_stability <- \(boot, level = NULL) {
  s <- itemStability(boot, IS.plot = FALSE)
  if (!is.null(level)) s <- s[[level]]
  stability <- s$item.stability$empirical.dimensions
  tibble(item      = names(stability),
         community = as.integer(s$membership$empirical[item]),
         stability = unname(stability))
}

# drop the items below the rule and bootstrap the rest again, until every
# item reaches the rule (at most 25 passes); returns each pass and the
# stability of the items that stay
converge_ega <- \(items, rule = .60, pass = 1) {
  stability <- item_stability(boot_ega(items))
  dropped   <- stability$item[stability$stability < rule]
  this_pass <- tibble(pass, items_in = ncol(items),
                      below = length(dropped),
                      min_stability  = min(stability$stability),
                      mean_stability = mean(stability$stability),
                      dropped = list(dropped))
  if (length(dropped) == 0 || pass == 25) {
    return(list(passes = this_pass, stability = stability))
  }
  rest <- converge_ega(select(items, -all_of(dropped)), rule, pass + 1)
  rest$passes <- bind_rows(this_pass, rest$passes)
  rest
}

# hierarchical EGA of one wave: communities of items (lower order) and
# communities of the community scores (higher order)
hier_seeds <- c(T0 = 123, T1 = 456, T2 = 789, T3 = 101112)

hier_ega <- \(items, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  hierEGA(items, scores = "network", loading.method = "revised",
          corr = "auto", na.data = "pairwise", model = "glasso",
          plot.EGA = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
}

hier_assignment <- \(hier) {
  hier$dim.variables |>
    as_tibble() |>
    transmute(item = items, lower = as.integer(lower),
              higher = as.integer(higher))
}

hier_size <- \(hier) {
  tibble(lower  = hier$lower_order$n.dim,
         higher = hier$higher_order$n.dim,
         TEFI   = hier$TEFI)
}

# the share of item pairs that two partitions treat alike (both together or
# both apart): 1 if the partitions are the same, whatever their numbers
pair_agreement <- \(a, b) {
  together_a <- outer(a, a, "==")
  together_b <- outer(b, b, "==")
  mean((together_a == together_b)[upper.tri(together_a)])
}

# a bootstrap of the hierarchical solution
boot_hier_ega <- \(items) {
  set.seed(42)
  bootEGA(items, iter = 500, type = "parametric", corr = "auto",
          model = "glasso", na.data = "pairwise", EGA.type = "hierEGA",
          scores = "network", loading.method = "revised", seed = 42,
          ncores = 1, verbose = FALSE, plot.itemStability = FALSE)
}

# item stability at both levels, in the order of the communities
hier_item_stability <- \(boot) {
  inner_join(item_stability(boot, "lower_order"),
             item_stability(boot, "higher_order"),
             by = "item", suffix = c("_lower", "_higher")) |>
    rename(lower = community_lower, higher = community_higher) |>
    arrange(higher, lower, desc(stability_lower))
}

# how often each community is found again with exactly the same items
structural_consistency <- \(boot, level = NULL) {
  s <- dimensionStability(boot, IS.plot = FALSE)
  if (!is.null(level)) s <- s[[level]]
  consistency <- s$dimension.stability$structural.consistency
  tibble(community   = as.integer(names(consistency)),
         consistency = unname(consistency))
}

The bootstraps take a few minutes each and run in a script of their own, which also carries the steps of Chapters 17 and 18. This chapter reads its results.

# Post hoc psychometrics: the bootstraps and the chain of item selections
# of Chapters 16 to 18. The T0 questionnaires calibrate every step; the
# composites are bootstrapped again at each wave.
# Run from swt-website/ after Chapter 2:  Rscript scripts/structure_pipeline.R

source("R/packages.R")
source("R/settings.R")
df <- readRDS("cache/df.rds")           # one row per questionnaire (Chapter 2)
item_names <- names(select(df, ListenOther1:CompetenceNonFrustrated4))
source("R/structure_pool.R")            # item pruning (Chapter 15)
source("R/structure_ega.R")             # network analyses (Chapter 16)
source("R/structure_irt.R")             # redundancy and IRT (Chapter 17)
source("R/structure_composites.R")      # composites (Chapter 18)

# Chapter 16: bootstrap until every item is stable, then bootstrap the
# hierarchical solution of the stable items. The items are ordered by
# community and stability; louvain and the bootstrap draws depend on the
# order of the items.
pool      <- structure_pool(df)
converged <- converge_ega(items_at(df, "T0", pool))
stable    <- converged$stability |>
  arrange(community, desc(stability)) |>
  pull(item)
boot_hier <- boot_hier_ega(items_at(df, "T0", stable))

saveRDS(list(pool        = pool,
             passes      = converged$passes,
             stability   = converged$stability,
             stable      = stable,
             hier_items  = hier_item_stability(boot_hier),
             hier_lower  = structural_consistency(boot_hier, "lower_order"),
             hier_higher = structural_consistency(boot_hier, "higher_order")),
        "cache/structure_ega.rds")

# Chapter 17: GRM per community and UVA on the persons who answered all
# stable items; the communities come from the bootstrap above
communities <- hier_item_stability(boot_hier) |>
  select(item, community = lower, stability = stability_lower)
calibration <- items_at(df, "T0", communities$item) |> drop_na()
pruned      <- community_discrimination(calibration, communities) |>
  prune_items(redundant_sets(calibration))
final_pool  <- pruned |> filter(keep) |> pull(item)

saveRDS(list(pruned = pruned, final_pool = final_pool),
        "cache/structure_irt.rds")

# Chapter 18: the hierarchical solution of the final pool and its
# bootstrap; the composites of its communities, bootstrapped at each wave
final_T0   <- items_at(df, "T0", final_pool)
assignment <- hier_ega(final_T0, hier_seeds[["T0"]]) |>
  hier_assignment() |>
  arrange(higher, lower, item)
boot_final <- boot_hier_ega(final_T0)
composites <- composite_items(assignment)

boot_wave <- \(wave) boot_ega(composite_scores(df, composites, wave))
composite_boot <- tibble(wave = names(hier_seeds)) |>
  mutate(boot        = map(wave, boot_wave),
         n           = map_int(boot, \(b) b$EGA$n),
         dimensions  = map_int(boot, \(b) b$EGA$n.dim),
         stability   = map(boot, item_stability),
         consistency = map(boot, structural_consistency),
         frequency   = map(boot, \(b) as_tibble(b$frequency))) |>
  select(-boot)

saveRDS(list(assignment     = assignment,
             final_items    = hier_item_stability(boot_final),
             final_lower    = structural_consistency(boot_final,
                                                     "lower_order"),
             final_higher   = structural_consistency(boot_final,
                                                     "higher_order"),
             composite_boot = composite_boot),
        "cache/structure_final.rds")


ega <- readRDS("cache/structure_ega.rds")

title: 18. Final structure
text:
18.2 Bootstrap of the hierarchical solution
How robust is the final structure? The bootstraps of this chapter run in the script of Chapter 16:

# Post hoc psychometrics: the bootstraps and the chain of item selections
# of Chapters 16 to 18. The T0 questionnaires calibrate every step; the
# composites are bootstrapped again at each wave.
# Run from swt-website/ after Chapter 2:  Rscript scripts/structure_pipeline.R

source("R/packages.R")
source("R/settings.R")
df <- readRDS("cache/df.rds")           # one row per questionnaire (Chapter 2)
item_names <- names(select(df, ListenOther1:CompetenceNonFrustrated4))
source("R/structure_pool.R")            # item pruning (Chapter 15)
source("R/structure_ega.R")             # network analyses (Chapter 16)
source("R/structure_irt.R")             # redundancy and IRT (Chapter 17)
source("R/structure_composites.R")      # composites (Chapter 18)

# Chapter 16: bootstrap until every item is stable, then bootstrap the
# hierarchical solution of the stable items. The items are ordered by
# community and stability; louvain and the bootstrap draws depend on the
# order of the items.
pool      <- structure_pool(df)
converged <- converge_ega(items_at(df, "T0", pool))
stable    <- converged$stability |>
  arrange(community, desc(stability)) |>
  pull(item)
boot_hier <- boot_hier_ega(items_at(df, "T0", stable))

saveRDS(list(pool        = pool,
             passes      = converged$passes,
             stability   = converged$stability,
             stable      = stable,
             hier_items  = hier_item_stability(boot_hier),
             hier_lower  = structural_consistency(boot_hier, "lower_order"),
             hier_higher = structural_consistency(boot_hier, "higher_order")),
        "cache/structure_ega.rds")

# Chapter 17: GRM per community and UVA on the persons who answered all
# stable items; the communities come from the bootstrap above
communities <- hier_item_stability(boot_hier) |>
  select(item, community = lower, stability = stability_lower)
calibration <- items_at(df, "T0", communities$item) |> drop_na()
pruned      <- community_discrimination(calibration, communities) |>
  prune_items(redundant_sets(calibration))
final_pool  <- pruned |> filter(keep) |> pull(item)

saveRDS(list(pruned = pruned, final_pool = final_pool),
        "cache/structure_irt.rds")

# Chapter 18: the hierarchical solution of the final pool and its
# bootstrap; the composites of its communities, bootstrapped at each wave
final_T0   <- items_at(df, "T0", final_pool)
assignment <- hier_ega(final_T0, hier_seeds[["T0"]]) |>
  hier_assignment() |>
  arrange(higher, lower, item)
boot_final <- boot_hier_ega(final_T0)
composites <- composite_items(assignment)

boot_wave <- \(wave) boot_ega(composite_scores(df, composites, wave))
composite_boot <- tibble(wave = names(hier_seeds)) |>
  mutate(boot        = map(wave, boot_wave),
         n           = map_int(boot, \(b) b$EGA$n),
         dimensions  = map_int(boot, \(b) b$EGA$n.dim),
         stability   = map(boot, item_stability),
         consistency = map(boot, structural_consistency),
         frequency   = map(boot, \(b) as_tibble(b$frequency))) |>
  select(-boot)

saveRDS(list(assignment     = assignment,
             final_items    = hier_item_stability(boot_final),
             final_lower    = structural_consistency(boot_final,
                                                     "lower_order"),
             final_higher   = structural_consistency(boot_final,
                                                     "higher_order"),
             composite_boot = composite_boot),
        "cache/structure_final.rds")

title: 18. Final structure
text:
18.3 Composites
What does each community measure, and how reliably? A composite is the mean of a community’s answered items; it takes the short name of its scale. The functions:

# Composites of the final structure (Chapter 18): one score per community
# of the final item pool, their reliability, how the composites group into
# factors, and a table of every item. Needs R/structure_ega.R and
# R/structure_irt.R.

# a community takes the short name of its scale; a community that mixes
# scales is "Connection" (listening, being moved, being understood)
scale_short <- c(
  ListenOther = "Listen", ListenSelf = "Listen", KamaMuta = "KamaMuta",
  Understood = "Underst", Resonance = "Resonance", Rogerian = "Rogerian",
  ParadoxMindset = "Paradox", IntellectualHumility = "IntHumility",
  ToleranceDiversity = "Tolerance", Flourishing = "Flourishing",
  Empowerment = "Empowerment", AutonomySatisfaction = "AutonomySat",
  CompetenceSatisfaction = "CompetenceSat"
)

community_name <- \(items) {
  scale <- unique(str_remove(items, "[0-9]+$"))
  if (length(scale) > 1) return("Connection")
  unname(coalesce(scale_short[scale], scale))
}

# a factor is named after its communities
factor_name <- \(communities) {
  communities <- as.character(communities)
  case_when("Connection" %in% communities  ~ "Engagement",
            "Flourishing" %in% communities ~ "Well-being and agency",
            .default = str_flatten(communities, " & "))
}

# the items of each composite, in the order of the communities
composite_items <- \(assignment) {
  assignment |>
    arrange(lower) |>
    mutate(composite = community_name(item), .by = lower) |>
    mutate(composite = fct_inorder(composite))
}

# composite scores of one wave: the mean of the answered items
composite_scores <- \(data, composites, wave) {
  answers <- data |> filter(Occasion == wave)
  split(composites$item, composites$composite) |>
    map(\(items) rowMeans(answers[items], na.rm = TRUE)) |>
    as_tibble()
}

# Cronbach's alpha on the persons who answered every item
cronbach <- \(items) {
  items <- drop_na(items)
  k <- ncol(items)
  v <- var(items)
  k / (k - 1) * (1 - sum(diag(v)) / sum(v))
}

# the correlation of each item with the mean of the other items
item_rest <- \(items) {
  map_dbl(names(items), \(item) {
    rest <- rowMeans(items[setdiff(names(items), item)], na.rm = TRUE)
    cor(items[[item]], rest, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
  })
}

# Fisher information of each item of a GRM at three trait levels
item_information <- \(fit, theta = c(-2, 0, 2)) {
  items <- colnames(extract.mirt(fit, "data"))
  map(seq_along(items), \(i) {
    info <- iteminfo(extract.item(fit, i), Theta = matrix(theta))
    tibble(item = items[i], theta = theta, information = info)
  }) |>
    list_rbind()
}

title: 18. Final structure
text:
18.5 The master table
How good is each item? For the final structure: each item’s factor, composite, GRM discrimination a, Fisher information I(θ) at three trait levels (θ = −2, 0, +2, about two standard deviations below the mean, the mean, two above), and its correlation with the mean of the other items of its composite. The GRMs are fitted per composite with at least three items, on the T0 questionnaires that answer all its items.

  distinct(higher, composite) |>
  mutate(factor = factor_name(composite), .by = higher)

grm <- composites |>
  filter(n() >= 3, .by = composite) |>
  summarise(fit = list(grm_fit(items_T0[item])), .by = composite) |>
  mutate(reliability = map_dbl(fit, marginal_rxx),
         a           = map(fit, discrimination),
         information = map(fit, item_information))

  arrange(higher, lower) |>
  left_join(select(factors, composite, factor), by = "composite") |>

  left_join(grm |> select(a) |> unnest(a), by = "item") |>
  left_join(grm |> select(information) |> unnest(information) |>
              pivot_wider(names_from = theta, values_from = information,
                          names_prefix = "I_"),

title: 19. Training effects on the new structure
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Re-estimates the training effects on the structure found in the data (Chapter 18): two factors, Engagement and Well-being and agency, their ten communities, and the single item on life satisfaction. The questions are those of Part C: does the trained group gain more in each training window, and does the training reach well-being through engagement, in the same four windows as Chapter 12? A last section tests whether the two factors are measured the same way at all four waves, as a latent difference-in-differences would need. Exploratory: the structure was derived from the same questionnaires (at T0), so these results describe this sample and need replication. Feeds the post hoc section of the paper.

title: 19. Training effects on the new structure
text:
19.1 Scores of the new structure
Which items make up the new scores? Each factor score and each community score is the mean of a person’s answered items:

# Scores of the post hoc structure (Chapter 19): the two factors and the
# ten communities of Chapter 18, each the mean of a person's answered items.
# Needs R/structure_composites.R (composite_items(), factor_name()).

# item -> community (composite) -> factor, from the final structure
structure_map <- readRDS("cache/structure_final.rds")$assignment |>
  composite_items() |>
  mutate(factor = factor_name(unique(composite)), .by = higher) |>
  # column names without spaces: engagement, wellbeing_agency
  mutate(factor_score = if_else(factor == "Engagement", "engagement",
                                "wellbeing_agency"))

# the mean of the answered items, missing when none was answered
item_mean <- \(data, items) {
  m <- rowMeans(data[items], na.rm = TRUE)
  if_else(is.nan(m), NA, m)
}

# add the two factor scores and the ten composites (prefix new_)
add_new_scores <- \(data) {
  factors    <- split(structure_map$item, structure_map$factor_score)
  composites <- split(structure_map$item,
                      str_c("new_", structure_map$composite))
  data |>
    bind_cols(map(c(factors, composites), \(items) item_mean(data, items)) |>
                as_tibble())
}

# one row per person: the two factor scores at each wave, and the training
# indicators of Chapter 2
new_scores_wide <- \(data, wide) {
  data |>
    select(id, Occasion, engagement, wellbeing_agency) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = Occasion,
                values_from = c(engagement, wellbeing_agency)) |>
    left_join(select(wide, id, condition, train_eg, train_cg), by = "id")
}

# training -> engagement -> well-being and agency in one window, controlling
# for both scores at the start of the window
factor_mediation_model <- \(pre, post, treated) {
  before <- str_c(c("engagement_", "wellbeing_agency_"), pre)
  after  <- str_c(c("engagement_", "wellbeing_agency_"), post)
  controls <- str_c(before, collapse = " + ")
  c(str_c(after[1], " ~ a*", treated, " + ", controls),
    str_c(after[2], " ~ b*", after[1], " + c*", treated, " + ", controls),
    str_c(before[1], " ~~ ", before[2]),
    "indirect := a*b",
    "direct := c",
    "total := c + a*b") |>
    str_c(collapse = "\n")
}

# Measurement invariance of the two factors over the waves (19.6). Needs
# R/longitudinal_models.R (waves, at(), wave_pairs).

# the community scores that measure a factor, in the order of Chapter 18
indicators_of <- \(f) {
  communities <- structure_map |>
    filter(factor_score == f) |>
    distinct(composite) |>
    arrange(composite)
  str_c("new_", communities$composite)
}

# one row per person, in the order of `wide`: the ten community scores at
# each wave (new_Connection_T0, ...)
community_scores_wide <- \(data, wide) {
  scores <- data |>
    select(id, Occasion, starts_with("new_")) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = Occasion, values_from = starts_with("new_"),
                names_glue = "{.value}_{Occasion}")
  wide |>
    select(id) |>
    left_join(scores, by = "id")
}

# one factor per wave, its community scores as indicators (the first is
# the marker) and each score's residual correlated with itself over the
# waves; configural, metric (equal loadings) or scalar (equal intercepts,
# latent means free from T1 on), as in Chapter 7
factor_invariance_model <- \(f, level = c("configural", "metric",
                                          "scalar")) {
  level      <- match.arg(level)
  indicators <- indicators_of(f)
  labels <- if (level == "configural") rep("", length(indicators)) else
    str_c("lam", seq_along(indicators), "*")
  labels[1] <- "1*"
  loadings <- map_chr(waves, \(w) str_c(
    "F_", w, " =~ ", str_c(labels, at(indicators, w), collapse = " + ")))
  covariances <- map_chr(wave_pairs, \(p) str_c("F_", p[1], " ~~ F_", p[2]))
  means <- if (level == "scalar") {
    c("F_T0 ~ 0*1", str_c("F_", waves[-1], " ~ 1"))
  } else {
    str_c("F_", waves, " ~ 0*1")
  }
  intercepts <- if (level == "scalar") {
    imap(indicators, \(x, j) str_c(at(x, waves), " ~ tau", j, "*1")) |>
      unlist()
  } else {
    character()
  }
  across_waves <- map(indicators, \(x) map_chr(wave_pairs, \(p)
    str_c(at(x, p[1]), " ~~ ", at(x, p[2])))) |> unlist()
  c(loadings, covariances, means, intercepts, across_waves) |>
    str_c(collapse = "\n")
}

The indirect effect through Engagement is 0.201 [0.117, 0.303] while the experimental group trains (Model 1) and 0.192 [0.087, 0.309] while the control group trains (Model 4); both intervals exclude 0. Between the trainings (Models 2 and 3) the indirect effects are small and their intervals include 0, as in Chapter 12. While the experimental group trains, the direct path is not significant (c = 0.10) and the total effect is (0.30, p = .003): an indirect-only mediation (Zhao et al., 2010), with a total effect that the preregistered composites do not show in this window (Chapter 12.3). 20.1 Three estimates of the training effect
Where do the methods agree? While the experimental group trains (T0 to T1), the effect of each scale in three estimates: the descriptive Δd (Chapter 9), the preregistered multilevel interaction at T1 (Chapter 10) and the latent difference-in-differences (Chapter 11, only where the scale is measured invariantly over time, Chapter 7). methods counts the estimates that are significant (p < .05) in favour of the training.

significant_up <- \(estimate, p) !is.na(p) & p < .05 & estimate > 0

  select(outcome = scale, label, block) |>

title: 20. Synthesis
text:
20.2 The wait-list replication
Does the effect return when the control group trains? The mirrored estimates for T2 to T3 (negative: the control group gains more):

# scales with a significant effect of the trained group in one window
count_dd <- \(from, to, sign) means$effects |>
  filter(pre == from, post == to, outcome %in% scales$scale, p < .05,
         sign * delta_d > 0) |>
  nrow()
count_piecewise <- \(group, sign) multilevel$piecewise |>
  filter(training == group, outcome %in% scales$scale, p < .05,
         sign * b > 0) |>
  nrow()
count_latent <- \(estimate, p, sign) smm$training_effects |>
  filter(scalar, .data[[p]] < .05, sign * .data[[estimate]] > 0) |>
  nrow()

replication <- tibble(
  estimate = c("Δd (Chapter 9)", "piecewise model (Chapter 10)",
               "latent DiD (Chapter 11)"),
  experimental_trains = c(count_dd("T0", "T1", 1),
                          count_piecewise("experimental", 1),

  control_trains      = c(count_dd("T2", "T3", -1),

title: 20. Synthesis
text:
20.4 Where the results are fragile
What limits these conclusions?

limits <- tibble(
  limit = c("latent models at a boundary (Chapter 11)",
            "constructs without scalar invariance over time (Chapter 7)",
            "constructs not scalar invariant across groups (Chapter 7)",
            "sample sets in which H2 misses significance (Chapter 14)",
            "mover contrasts significant (Chapter 13)",
            "scales with a Δd for the training after BH correction (Chapter 9)",
            "latent training effects after BH correction (Chapter 11)"),
  n = c(sum(!smm$admissible$admissible),
        sum(!invariance$summary$scalar),
        sum(invariance$groups$Chen != "scalar"),
        robustness$delta_d |>
          filter(outcome == "H2_CognitiveComplexity", pre == "T0",
                 post == "T1", p >= .05) |> nrow(),
        movers$window_rates |> distinct(score, pre, p) |>
          filter(p < .05) |> nrow(),
        means$corrected |>

Seven of the 22 latent models end at a boundary (autocorrelated residuals beyond ±1 or negative residual variances), so their latent estimates are read with caution. Two constructs are not measured invariantly over time, and Autonomy Satisfaction joins them under the stricter cutoffs for small samples (Chapter 7.3). Before the training, 9 of the 22 constructs are not measured alike in the two groups, among them Rogerian Schema, Paradox Mindset, and Relatedness Satisfaction, which show the effect in all three estimates; their latent effects assume equal measurement in both groups. By Cohen’s labels the latent effects are small (Chapter 11.7).
Correcting for testing 23 scales at once (Benjamini-Hochberg) leaves 1 scale with a Δd for the training and 6 of the eight latent training effects; tested one-sided, as the hypotheses are directional, all three composites show the multilevel effect at T1. With the standard deviation of all questionnaires before the window, the replication while the control group trains shrinks from 9 to 5 scales (Chapter 9.4). Other choices leave the picture in place: a trainer level adds nothing to the multilevel models (Chapter 10.2), and dropout does not explain the late gains in well-being (Chapter 9.6). Δd and the latent models leave out that persons are clustered in municipalities; the multilevel models, which take the municipalities into account, and the cluster-robust mediation give the same picture.
The effect on Cognitive Complexity holds in eight of nine sample sets and misses significance only among the 127 persons with all four waves. At the level of single persons, no scale separates the groups significantly (Chapter 13). The post hoc structure was found in the same data and partly selected for responsiveness to the training, and neither of its two factors is scalar invariant over the waves (Chapter 19.6), so its effects rest on manifest scores and need a new sample.

title: 8. Simultaneous block models
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Chapters 6 and 7 model each construct alone. Here all constructs of one hypothesis block enter one factor model, which answers two questions a single construct cannot: are the constructs of a block empirically distinct (discriminant validity), and does the block as a whole stay invariant over time? Large models of this kind often end at a boundary, so the chapter closes with the admissibility of every solution. Feeds the discriminant-validity paragraph and the block-level invariance table of the supplement.
source("R/packages.R")                  # all packages (Chapter 1)
source("R/settings.R")                  # waves, conditions, folders (Chapter 1)
df      <- readRDS("cache/df.rds")      # one row per questionnaire (Chapter 2)
df_wide <- readRDS("cache/df_wide.rds") # one row per person (Chapter 2)
item_names <- names(select(df, ListenOther1:CompetenceNonFrustrated4))
source("R/scales.R")                    # the 23 scales (Chapter 2)
source("R/measurement.R")               # models of the constructs (Chapter 6)
source("R/longitudinal_models.R")       # waves, at() (Chapter 7)

title: 8. Simultaneous block models
text:
8.1 The block models
How is a block modelled? Each construct keeps its measurement model of Chapter 6, now with marker identification throughout: the first item’s loading is 1, also for the two-item constructs, which the other factors of the block identify without equal loadings. Understood enters Listening and Togetherness as a factor with a single item. All factors of a block correlate freely. Over several waves, each construct has one factor per wave, and each item’s residual correlates with itself across the waves, as in Chapter 7. The metric level holds the loadings, the scalar level also the intercepts equal over the waves.

# Simultaneous block models (Chapter 8): all constructs of one hypothesis
# block in one factor model, at one wave or over several waves. Marker
# identification throughout, also for the two-item constructs; Understood
# enters H1 as a single-item factor (loading 1, residual variance 0).
# Needs R/measurement.R and R/longitudinal_models.R (at(), waves).

blocks <- list(
  H1 = c("ListenOther", "ListenSelf", "Understood", "KamaMuta", "Resonance",
         "Belongingness", "NoAlienation", "NoIsolation"),
  H2 = c("Rogerian", "ParadoxMindset", "IntellectualHumility",
         "ToleranceDiversity", "womenAttitude"),
  H3 = c("Flourishing", "AutonomySatisfaction", "RelatednessSatisfaction",
         "CompetenceSatisfaction", "AutonomyNonFrustrated",
         "RelatednessNonFrustrated", "CompetenceNonFrustrated", "Empowerment",
         "Agency", "IntellectualCapital")
)
block_items <- c(model_items, list(Understood = "Understood1"))

# all items of a block, as plain names
items_of <- \(block) list_c(block_items[block])

# one wave, long data: one factor per construct, all factors correlated
block_wave_model <- \(block) {
  pairs <- residual_pairs |> filter(construct %in% block)
  c(map_chr(block, \(c)
      str_c(c, " =~ 1*", str_c(block_items[[c]], collapse = " + "))),
    if ("Understood" %in% block) "Understood1 ~~ 0*Understood1",
    str_c(pairs$item_a, " ~~ ", pairs$item_b)) |>
    str_c(collapse = "\n")
}

# several waves, wide data: one factor per construct and wave; metric holds
# the loadings (l_), scalar also the intercepts (t_) equal over the waves
block_long_model <- \(block, level = c("configural", "metric", "scalar"),
                      over = waves) {
  level <- match.arg(level)
  pairs <- residual_pairs |> filter(construct %in% block)

  per_construct <- map(block, \(c) {
    items <- block_items[[c]]
    labels <- if (level == "configural") rep("", length(items)) else
      str_c("l_", c, seq_along(items), "*")
    labels[1] <- "1*"
    factor <- str_c(c, "_", over)
    c(
      # loadings
      map2_chr(factor, over, \(f, w)
        str_c(f, " =~ ", str_c(labels, at(items, w), collapse = " + "))),
      # a single item carries its factor without error
      if (length(items) == 1) str_c(at(items, over), " ~~ 0*", at(items, over)),
      # intercepts (scalar) and latent means: 0, free after the first wave
      # at the scalar level
      if (level == "scalar") {
        imap(items, \(item, j) str_c(at(item, over), " ~ t_", c, j, "*1")) |>
          unlist()
      },
      str_c(factor, " ~ ", if (level == "scalar") {
        c("0*1", rep("1", length(over) - 1))
      } else {
        "0*1"
      }),
      # autocorrelated residuals of multi-item constructs
      if (length(items) > 1) {
        map(items, \(item) map_chr(combn(over, 2, simplify = FALSE), \(p)
          str_c(at(item, p[1]), " ~~ ", at(item, p[2])))) |>
          unlist()
      }
    )
  }) |>
    unlist()

  # residual covariances within each wave
  within_waves <- map2(pairs$item_a, pairs$item_b, \(a, b)
    str_c(at(a, over), " ~~ ", at(b, over))) |> unlist()

  c(per_construct, within_waves) |> str_c(collapse = "\n")
}
